title: China's Baidu reports 15% revenue growth, beating expectations
text:
BEIJING — Chinese tech company Baidu on Tuesday reported better-than-expected revenue, up by 15% year-on-year in the second quarter and bolstered by growth in advertising.
This was the fastest quarterly year-on-year growth pace in two years, according to Refinitiv data.
Baidu's U.S.-traded shares were up by more than 4% in pre-market trading.
Here's how Baidu did in the June quarter versus Refinitiv consensus estimates:
- Revenue: 34.1 billion yuan ($4.7 billion) versus 33.28 billion yuan expected.
Within Baidu's core businesses, online marketing revenue rose by 15% to 19.6 billion yuan in the second quarter, and non-online marketing revenue added 12% to 6.8 billion yuan.
Earnings per American Depositary Share on a non-GAAP basis were 22.55 yuan, versus 15.79 yuan in the year-ago period.
"In the second quarter of 2023, Baidu Core accelerated revenue and profit growth, driven by the solid performance of online marketing business and operating leverage," said Robin Li, Co-founder and CEO of Baidu, said in a release.
"Generative AI and large language models hold immense transformative power in numerous industries, presenting a significant market opportunity for us," he said.
Baidu has been making progress with a Chinese-language ChatGPT alternative called Ernie bot, which is open to the public and was launched in March. OpenAI's wildly popular rival chatbot isn't easily accessible in the country.
Last week, Baidu announced that five Ernie bot plugins — including ones for quickly converting text to video and for PDF search — would become more widely available to users. Three of the plugins can also be used simultaneously, according to the company.
Baidu last week also revealed an AI-powered assistant that could help with tasks including booking meetings, air tickets and hotels. It was not immediately clear how users could obtain the assistant product.
The company is also looking to expand the reach of AI into the automobile sector. This month, the company announced a strategic agreement with state-owned Changan Automobile to develop autonomous driving capabilities based on the AI model behind Baidu's Ernie bot.
Baidu is not alone in its foray, as other Chinese tech giants are also pushing into AI-related products. Earlier this month, e-commerce giant Alibaba claimed that "strong demand" for training artificial intelligence models on the cloud and the related business opportunity was just beginning.
Internet titan Tencent said during its earnings release last week that it plans to launch its own AI model later this year, for use in products such as gaming and advertising.
Robotaxi business
Baidu also operates self-driving taxis under the Apollo Go brand in China. In the second quarter, Baidu said it ran roughly 714,000 robotaxi rides, up from 660,000 in the first quarter.
The company was allowed to start charging fares for public robotaxi rides in Beijing in November 2021. Passengers can book the rides, which are typically highly subsidized, via an app.
Most of the robotaxis, which are available in parts of many major Chinese cities, still have human staff inside.
In June, the company said it received approval to operate robotaxis without employees in a suburb of Shenzhen. That followed similar approval in August 2022 to remove human staff in some robotaxis in parts of Wuhan and Chongqing.

title: Council Post: Content In Context: The Foundation For Modern Knowledge Management
text:
Antti Nivala is Founder and CEO of M-Files, a global leader in information management.
For organizations looking to leverage data for business-critical decision management, knowledge management is critical. Data in a silo does not drive value, but when we dig into the context behind the data, we can drive maximum value for the enterprise. However, isolating context from data poses multiple challenges—from fragmentation, silos and security. These roadblocks often make it difficult to extract the proper context needed to make smart decisions
Metadata: The King Of Context
To gain context from content, you need to start with metadata. Metadata is the data that describes other data—creating the ability to sort and identify the attributes of whatever it is describing, such as what the document is about, what it is related to or who has last worked on it.
The best way to start thinking about metadata is to think of the different contexts your business runs in. The work you do is typically associated with one or more business entities, such as a client, project, department, employee, asset, etc. Most likely, it is a combination of several of those entities.
For each of those entities, it’s important to understand the information related to them. For instance, where your customers are located, how long they have been a customer, their current status, point-of-contact and so on. The metadata structure you create is then just a reflection of those business entities and contexts.
Getting started on building out a metadata model is as simple as looking at the folder structures the organization has created. This won’t provide the full picture since folders are limited to organizing things into one context, but it’s a good starting point.
The precise tagging of metadata is what allows cognitive search engines to effectively function, allowing employees to easily find what they are looking for in one place. In addition, the implementation of metadata contributes to improved business intelligence, opportunities for new revenue streams, support for auditing processes and more.
For example, metadata can help manage the proliferation of generative AI tools. By utilizing metadata tags prohibiting the use of sensitive or secret data in large language models, organizations can avoid content being purposefully or inadvertently shared with these tools.
AI For Context
AI is a hot topic, not just when it comes to content or image creation, but the potential it has to supercharge knowledge management.
With AI, it really helps to have a defined metadata model. Especially if you want to leverage AI to better understand content. The more the AI is trained on the way you do your work, the better it will be at doing tasks like automatically classifying documents, extracting important information, protecting confidential information and so on.
The first step is identifying the areas where AI will bring the most value to your users. For example, if your organization works with large volumes of information and you are having trouble finding answers or the right information, AI-assisted semantic search or question/answer using generative AI could potentially help.
It’s also important to understand that the field is changing rapidly. In just six months we’ve seen the entire landscape change with advancements in generative AI and the use of large language models like GPT. However, these tools can open organizations to security risks and may introduce unintended biases. Therefore, it’s important to have internal experts, a trusted vendor or a partner to work with when evaluating the best ways to solve specific business problems with AI.
Organizing content based on end-user role or business context is what powers smart automation that minimizes human error, drives efficiencies and mitigates risk, especially in heavily regulated industries, such as financial services. AI-powered automation, similar to the application of metadata, further reduces the amount of resources knowledge workers must spend simply managing data. This frees them up to focus on more critical tasks, leading to better customer experiences.
Contextual Search For Enhanced Productivity
Cognitive search is by nature contextual, allowing users to pose a query in natural language, and in return, the engine provides resources highly suited to the users’ needs. With cognitive search, as with semantic search, we eliminate the need for “keywords.” Thus we are able to access resources that are related to our query, but maybe not obviously so. This, then, reduces time employees need to search for information so that they can focus on more pressing tasks that drive higher value for the organization.
Not every organization will need cognitive search as it is a more technical solution, but for those who are dealing with a deluge of content, it is an important tool for information management.
DIY For Knowledge Management
If you are a Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace customer, one DIY option would be to start with the tools provided by those solutions. Both Microsoft and Google provide methods for organizing content in folder or site hierarchies, and both have functionality to manage different versions and share content.
The other advantage is they are tightly integrated into the productivity tools a lot of people use like Teams, Outlook and Gmail. For larger organizations, there will be limitations with managing content in multiple contexts, creating automated permissions and automating processes, but this is a suitable option for smaller companies or those just starting their knowledge management journey.
The importance of context in content cannot be overstated. It’s only when data is presented in a contextual way that it becomes true knowledge. One need only look to the proliferation of cognitive search powered by artificial intelligence (AI) to know if this is the case. As the adoption of technology speeds up, so does the need for data that is easy to find, simple to tag and relevant to user or business needs. Context in content is not only something businesses should simply consider, but something they should make a priority if they want to harness any of the new technologies rapidly becoming available.

title: Council Post: Does Your Business Need Protection From AI?
text:
CEO, Founder at KeyMedia Solutions. We are curious problem solvers helping SMBs achieve success through online advertising.
Since the public launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, chances are good that artificial intelligence has been the hottest topic around your company watercooler, if not in the C-suite, then among your staff. I would even bet that they are using it at a greater rate than you are aware of. To test this and gain a better understanding of how my staff was using AI, I surveyed my team recently and learned that 90% were using AI to assist in writing (emails, notes, proposals, marketing content) and 75% were using AI for some form of design or concepting.
At first, I was thrilled that they are grabbing hold of new technology, asking questions and testing. This is all critical to the advancement of our company in a highly competitive industry.
Then, I started thinking more deeply about the trend that was evolving and started to become concerned. We did not have a written policy governing the team’s testing and use. We did not have written guidelines or boundaries to monitor the data flow or protect them and the company. So we created an AI policy, along with a best practice checklist and a document listing safe AI tools and a "do not use" list.
While AI can offer many benefits to companies, there are also potential dangers you need to address to protect your business and its stakeholders.
Potential Dangers Of AI
Some of the potential dangers can include:
Data Security And Privacy Concerns
AI tools often require access to data to learn and improve, which raises concerns about data security and privacy. If your employees experiment with AI tools without proper safeguards, sensitive company and customer data could be exposed, leading to potential legal and financial liabilities.
Intellectual Property Risks
If employees use proprietary company data or software to train AI models without authorization, it could lead to intellectual property infringement issues. This may result in disputes over ownership and control of the AI models, affecting the company's competitive advantage.
Regulatory Compliance
Depending on the industry, there may be specific regulations that govern the handling of data. Unauthorized experimentation with AI could lead to violations of these regulations, resulting in fines and reputational damage.
Bias And Fairness
AI models trained on biased data can perpetuate and amplify existing biases, leading to discriminatory outcomes. If your employees experiment with AI without considering fairness and inclusivity, it could lead to discrimination issues and damage the company's reputation. This is especially risky if they are not trained in bias.
Unreliable Outputs
AI models, including ChatGPT, can generate incorrect or misleading information. Relying on unreliable AI-generated outputs without fact-checking procedures could lead to poor decision making and operational inefficiencies.
Miscommunication With Customers
If AI-generated content is shared with customers without proper oversight, it could lead to miscommunication, confusion and customer dissatisfaction.
Potential Liability For AI Actions
It's possible that AI systems could take actions that have legal consequences. If an employee deploys an AI tool that interacts with customers or external stakeholders and causes harm, the company could be held liable for those actions.
How To Protect Your Business
To mitigate these dangers, make sure you establish clear AI usage policies, ensure that only authorized personnel have access to sensitive data, and provide proper training on AI ethics and best practices. Regular monitoring and auditing of AI usage can also help you identify and address potential risks early on. Additionally, collaborating with legal and AI experts can help you understand and navigate the legal and ethical complexities of AI adoption.
This isn't a task that can be pushed down the priority list. Over the last few weeks, I have had multiple conversations with business owners who have experienced some of these dangers in their shops. Whether you think you need to address AI usage today or next year, start the conversation today and find a resource available to help develop these new policies.

title: Council Post: AI: The Ultimate Force Multiplier For Small Business Success
text:
Jason Cross is the SVP, Digital Presence and Commerce, at Newfold Digital; Jason has a long history of assisting SMBs.
AI gives entrepreneurs and business owners more innovation, creativity, problem-solving and personalization. AI-driven tools made to bring ideas to life with efficient and effective content generation promise to revolutionize how we think about starting and growing a business.
Both powerful and accessible, AI-powered tools can be an entrepreneur’s best friend, taking on the role of a brainstorming partner, content creator and business accelerator. Just as the internet permanently transformed how we do business, companies are making the most of AI and integrating its capabilities into everyday practices like search—making search engine optimization (SEO) even more vital. While AI continues to evolve, here are a few advantages that entrepreneurs and side hustlers can use right now.
Lowered Barriers To Entry
Small or independent businesses often need to catch up when new technologies are introduced, with high-cost barriers giving larger competitors more opportunities to engage with emerging tech in its early stages. But with AI tools increasingly affordable for everyday use, their growth potential is democratized. Using AI technology, small-business owners have not only evened the playing field with enterprises but now have an adaptability advantage over them.
The reason why is simple: A business with a handful of employees is more adaptable to new AI-backed strategies and behaviors than an industry giant. It can more efficiently capitalize on the benefits these tools have to offer.
AI helps address the pain points that affect smaller businesses most acutely, like creating website content or providing robust and timely customer support. Responsibly automating those tasks can accelerate the growth process for new and small businesses, streamlining the more foundational aspects of everyday operations, leaving more time for innovation, and allowing limited budgets to stretch further by helping employees learn and manage various tasks.
Improved Internal And External Experiences
Many small-business owners are running the show independently, and with so many different responsibilities to account for, it’s easy to be overwhelmed, especially at the outset. According to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, over 20% of small businesses fail within the first year. When extended to five years, that figure grows to nearly 50%.
When competing with brands that have more access to capital and the luxury of offering lower pricing, small businesses need to win out the customer experience. Luckily, AI can play an active role in helping them to do so, freeing up time and resources to allow humans to engage with human problems and automate more administrative, predictable tasks.
AI-powered chatbots are a common asset in enhancing customer service by taking on less intricate queries, so entrepreneurs can focus on big-picture goals. From a customer standpoint, it means less time on hold, quicker resolution for support issues, and a more tailored experience optimized for their needs. Meanwhile, new innovations such as ChatGPT (and other LLMs) give small businesses access to affordable solutions that streamline the creation of digital content. Leveraging the power of AI to automate more administrative tasks helps small businesses focus efforts in areas where human traits—such as empathy and critical thinking—are specifically needed to advance growth and brand reputation.
More Effective Marketing
Marketing relies heavily on intuition and research, and while entrepreneurs may have the former, the latter can be challenging to come by with limited resources. The best campaigns are rooted in common sense but backed by data, with companies putting themselves in their customer’s shoes to understand what they’re looking for.
An emerging trend in this space is leveraging AI for market research, a task that many aspiring entrepreneurs often lack the skills or resources to perform. Thanks to AI, this essential step of acquiring and retaining customers becomes more accessible. Historically a time-consuming and resource-intensive practice, insightful data analysis promises to be more efficient and cost-effective with the help of AI.
While findings and figures should always be double-checked, given that these tools are fallible, the ability to interact with powerful AI-powered tools can help entrepreneurs and SMB marketing leaders establish credibility and campaign viability, whether by affirming existing stances or pointing out any logical missteps. AI’s marketing benefits extend beyond everyday initiatives.
AI tools can aid small businesses in coming up with more creative business and domain names, as well as search-engine-optimized website copy, making up for a lack of marketing expertise on the part of the entrepreneur. By utilizing AI to analyze website traffic and where customers are spending the most time online, targeted marketing strategies can be identified and implemented much more effectively.
Multiplying Your Efforts
The military term “force multiplication” refers to the capacity for a particular technology, type of tactics or circumstances to provide an advantage that would only be gained through greater numbers. In other words, a force multiplier makes up for a need for more personnel.
While AI-powered tools can’t fully replace human employees, they can multiply the force of the small-business owner or entrepreneur by providing them with a distinct technological advantage. As the internet has revolutionized communication, information access and global connectivity, AI is poised to reshape the way we interact with technology, solve problems and arrive at decisions. The better you understand and can utilize AI tools, the greater this multiplying factor will be.
As a small-business owner, your unique skills, talents and areas of expertise make you stand out. AI can augment these strengths as a supportive tool in your arsenal. This technology can help bridge the gap between smaller-scale operations and the extensive resources of larger competitors. By maximizing the use of AI as a force multiplier, specifically for tasks like marketing, improving customer experiences, content creation and beyond, you can secure a competitive position in the SMB sector for the foreseeable future.

title: Council Post: Generative AI: Accelerating Business Transformation Across Industries
text:
Senior vice president of D2C at ITC Infotech.
The capacity of generative AI to automate and execute language-based tasks at high speed and efficiency is contributing to its emerging status as a transformative force in the business landscape. While it's still in the early stages of widespread adoption, businesses are starting to recognize its potential in enhancing operations, enriching customer engagement and bolstering overall efficiency.
Decoding Unstructured Data: The Core Strength Of Generative AI
The core strength of generative AI lies in its ability to analyze unstructured data—data that doesn't adhere to a fixed format or model, such as text, images, audio, video and social media posts. The complexity and variability of unstructured data, filled with ambiguities, nuances and contextual layers, make it a rich source of potential insights. A prime example of this is customer reviews, an unstructured data form, which often reveals customer sentiments, preferences and improvement areas not immediately discernible from structured data sources.
Potential Use Cases
Generative AI can be used to interpret raw consumer feedback from various platforms, such as Amazon, and derive insights from this data, spotlighting potential areas for product or service improvement based on customer suggestions. This capability streamlines understanding of customer sentiments, leading to improved product development and superior consumer experiences.
Generative AI can also potentially be a game changer in personalized email marketing campaigns when combined with discriminative (traditional) machine learning algorithms. Businesses can construct more strategic and engaging marketing campaigns by leveraging the insights from machine learning-based customer profiling along with generative AI’s ability to create personalized content.
Another potential use of generative AI lies in automating labor-intensive tasks such as preparing sales reports, drafting and reviewing contract terms, and supporting reporting operations. Culling out ESG numbers for regulatory reporting and compliance is a very cumbersome task. Generative AI can be very handy in automating this task when combined with other intelligent document processing techniques. Generative AI may also be useful for reviewing contracts, highlighting potential conflict of interest clauses and drafting terms to expedite the contract process. In examining these often text-heavy documents, generative AI can identify trends, anomalies or crucial points of interest that may otherwise be overlooked, thus aiding in strategic planning and decision-making.
Navigating The Challenges
Implementing generative AI solutions isn't without its challenges. Large language models (LLMs) and large multimodal models (LMMs) have occasionally disseminated false, outdated and discriminatory information with a level of conviction that could mislead even the most critical readers. This issue, however, can be mitigated by ensuring that these models are trained with the most recent and verified data, thus offering a viable strategy to sidestep this problem.
Generative AI has also been used to create deepfake images and videos. This warrants a need for responsible, trustworthy, ethical and safe AI solutions. The value of these solutions lies in their consistent performance at scale, making rigorous testing and validation a necessity to prevent operational disruptions, revenue losses and potential reputational damage due to unintended consequences.
Another challenge lies in managing AI hallucinations, a significant obstacle in the widespread adoption of large language models. Using outputs from these models, especially in high-stake contexts, requires careful consideration and protocols. Evaluations of model grounding and fine-grained evaluations can help manage this issue by assessing the model's ability to produce outputs supported by given context or input data and identifying specific components where hallucinations may occur. Additionally, reliable and diverse internal data sets can significantly upgrade the reliability of AI-generated outputs. Model regularization penalizes AI behaviors that deviate from company norms, ensuring consistent outputs. A touch of human oversight, where in-house experts vet AI-generated content, can be the linchpin to bridging the gap between AI capabilities and company expectations.
Setting clear AI operational boundaries across departments, whether in finance, marketing or customer service, safeguards against irrelevant or off-mark AI suggestions. Furthermore, a clear departmental understanding of the AI tools at their disposal, complemented by regular training sessions, can significantly cut down inconsistencies.
To ensure consistent and effective generative AI performance, implementing key evaluation metrics is a crucial step. For instance, in language modeling, measures such as perplexity and cross-entropy loss provide insights into the model's proficiency in predicting the probability distribution of test data, and the divergence between its predicted and true distributions respectively. In the field of machine translation, BLEU, METEOR and TER are key metrics, each quantifying different aspects of the translation's quality such as the amount of editing required to match a reference translation.
Generative AI's understanding and reasoning about natural language are assessed using evaluations like pronoun disambiguation, Winograd Schema Challenge, text entailment, etc. testing the AI’s ability to interpret context, recognize relationships and infer meanings, which are crucial to generate meaningful and coherent text. Metrics like these ensure a company's AI system is aligned with its specific needs and capable of delivering reliable, high-quality results.
Depending on the use and implementation of generative AI, there could be exposure to intellectual property or trade secrets, increasing the risk of fraud. It's vital to maintain vigilance to ensure AI usage doesn't contravene applicable laws (including privacy laws), client agreements or professional standards.
In summary, generative AI presents a progressive approach to leveraging the value of unstructured data for industrial use. While there are measures available to control hallucinations, further research, rigorous testing and careful implementation are needed to fully unlock generative AI's potential.

text:

SoftBank’s arm files for IPO that is set to be 2023’s biggest
In a long-awaited regulatory filing Monday, Arm said the offering is being led by Barclays Plc, Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Mizuho Financial Group Inc.
SoftBank Group Corp.’s Arm Holdings Ltd. took a step toward what’s set to become the biggest US initial public offering of the year, a bet that the once-obscure designer of phone chips can flourish in the era of artificial intelligence computing.
In a long-awaited regulatory filing Monday, Arm said the offering is being led by Barclays Plc, Goldman Sachs Group Inc., JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Mizuho Financial Group Inc. The document listed 24 other underwriters below that top tier — with Morgan Stanley notably absent.
A successful debut by Arm would provide a windfall for SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son, whose Vision Fund lost a record $30 billion last year. It could also spur dozens of companies to pursue — or further delay — their own IPO plans. That includes businesses like online grocery-delivery firm Instacart Inc., marketing and data automation provider Klaviyo and footwear maker Birkenstock.
Arm plans to start its roadshow the first week of September and price the IPO the following week, Bloomberg has reported. The company didn’t disclose proposed terms for the share sale in the document, but it’s expected to seek a valuation of $60 billion to $70 billion. Arm, based in Cambridge, UK, also has held talks with some of its biggest customers about backing the IPO.
While Arm had been aiming to raise $8 billion to $10 billion in the IPO, that target could be lower since SoftBank has decided to hold onto more of the company after buying Vision Fund’s stake in it. That transaction valued Arm at more than $64 billion, based on the filing.
Even so, the offering promises to give the struggling IPO market its biggest lift in almost two years. The listing is poised to be the largest in the US since electric-vehicle maker Rivian Automotive Inc.’s $13.7 billion offering in October 2021. It could rank near or even just below the tech industry’s largest-ever IPOs: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s $25 billion 2014 offering and 2012’s $16 billion debut by Meta Platforms Inc., then known as Facebook Inc.
Arm’s target valuation reflects a belief that it will benefit from the stampede toward artificial intelligence chips and generative AI — an industry shift that has helped give chipmaker Nvidia Corp. a $1.2 trillion valuation.
“A strong performance from Arm will not only be a major windfall for SoftBank, but also reinforce its AI strategy by showing the market hype around AI hasn’t waned,” said Kyle Stanford, an analyst at PitchBook.
Though Arm’s technology is used in almost every smartphone, it isn’t well-known among consumers. Arm sells the blueprints needed to design microprocessors, and licenses technology known as instruction sets that dictate how software programs communicate with those chips. The power efficiency of Arm’s technology helped make it ubiquitous on phones, where battery life is critical.
Rene Haas, who took over as Arm’s chief executive officer last year, is now working to expand beyond the smartphone market, which has stagnated in recent years. He’s setting his sights on more advanced computing, particularly the chips for data centers and AI applications.
Processors for that market are among the most expensive — and profitable — in the industry. Amazon.com Inc. has adopted Arm-based chips for its Amazon Web Services because it says they are more efficient both in terms of energy and economics. They are used by 40,000 AWS customers.
SoftBank will remain the controlling shareholder of Arm after it begins trading, according to the filing. SoftBank, based in Tokyo, has acquired substantially all of the Vision Fund’s 25% stake in Arm for $16.1 billion. The filing warned that this transaction might not be indicative of the Arm share price after the offering.
The paperwork also confirmed that Arm saw its revenue decline about 1% in its last fiscal year. The company’s sales fell to $2.68 billion for the year ended March 31, according to the document.
The overall chip industry is still contending with a sales slump, worsened by a glut of inventory. The smartphone market has been hit especially hard. Qualcomm Inc., one of Arm’s biggest customers, gave a disappointing forecast for the latest quarter earlier this month, sending its shares tumbling. And even Apple Inc.’s prized iPhone has seen demand slow.
Tensions with China also could cast a shadow over Arm’s business. In the filing, the company pointed to export restrictions from the US and UK as risks, hindering its ability to sell its Neoverse processor in China.
Arm plans to change its name to “Arm Holdings Plc” before it begins trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ARM. The filing confirms that the IPO’s top four banks will be acting as joint book-running managers of the offering. Bloomberg News has reported that the four will get an equal share of the fees, breaking with standard practice.
In the filing, Arm called itself an “engineering-first company,” with 4,753 of its workers — or about 80% of global employees — focused on research, design and technical innovation. The company said it owns or co-owns about 6,800 issued patents and has approximately 2,700 patent applications pending worldwide.
In the last fiscal year, more than 260 companies were using Arm-based chips, including Amazon, Alphabet Inc., Qualcomm and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. The company has worked with its top 10 customers — measured by royalty revenue — for an average of more than 20 years.
As AI fever has swept the tech industry, companies will need the right chips to run complex software. Arm says that every processor it designs will accelerate the AI and machine learning tech that it helps power. Its processors already run those technologies, and the company has started adding new functionality to make the algorithms run faster.
As part of that push, Arm is working with Alphabet, autonomous driving company Cruise, Mercedes-Benz, Meta and Nvidia to deploy Arm technology that can run AI-based software.
Arm was founded in 1990 as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple and VLSI Technology. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange and Nasdaq from 1998 until 2016, when SoftBank acquired the business for $32 billion.
SoftBank previously attempted to sell Arm to Nvidia in a $40 billion deal, which would have been the largest chip industry takeover. But the purchase faced opposition from regulators and Arm’s own customers, and Nvidia walked away from it last year. SoftBank then embarked on its plan for the IPO.

That includes businesses like online grocery-delivery firm Instacart Inc., marketing and data automation provider Klaviyo and footwear maker Birkenstock.

While Arm had been aiming to raise $8 billion to $10 billion in the IPO, that target could be lower since SoftBank has decided to hold onto more of the company after buying Vision Fund’s stake in it. That transaction valued Arm at more than $64 billion, based on the filing.
Even so, the offering promises to give the struggling IPO market its biggest lift in almost two years. The listing is poised to be the largest in the US since electric-vehicle maker Rivian Automotive Inc.’s $13.7 billion offering in October 2021. It could rank near or even just below the tech industry’s largest-ever IPOs: Alibaba Group Holding Ltd.’s $25 billion 2014 offering and 2012’s $16 billion debut by Meta Platforms Inc., then known as Facebook Inc.
Arm’s target valuation reflects a belief that it will benefit from the stampede toward artificial intelligence chips and generative AI — an industry shift that has helped give chipmaker Nvidia Corp. a $1.2 trillion valuation.
“A strong performance from Arm will not only be a major windfall for SoftBank, but also reinforce its AI strategy by showing the market hype around AI hasn’t waned,” said Kyle Stanford, an analyst at PitchBook.
Though Arm’s technology is used in almost every smartphone, it isn’t well-known among consumers. Arm sells the blueprints needed to design microprocessors, and licenses technology known as instruction sets that dictate how software programs communicate with those chips. The power efficiency of Arm’s technology helped make it ubiquitous on phones, where battery life is critical.
Rene Haas, who took over as Arm’s chief executive officer last year, is now working to expand beyond the smartphone market, which has stagnated in recent years. He’s setting his sights on more advanced computing, particularly the chips for data centers and AI applications.
Processors for that market are among the most expensive — and profitable — in the industry. Amazon.com Inc. has adopted Arm-based chips for its Amazon Web Services because it says they are more efficient both in terms of energy and economics. They are used by 40,000 AWS customers.
SoftBank will remain the controlling shareholder of Arm after it begins trading, according to the filing. SoftBank, based in Tokyo, has acquired substantially all of the Vision Fund’s 25% stake in Arm for $16.1 billion. The filing warned that this transaction might not be indicative of the Arm share price after the offering.
The paperwork also confirmed that Arm saw its revenue decline about 1% in its last fiscal year. The company’s sales fell to $2.68 billion for the year ended March 31, according to the document.
The overall chip industry is still contending with a sales slump, worsened by a glut of inventory. The smartphone market has been hit especially hard. Qualcomm Inc., one of Arm’s biggest customers, gave a disappointing forecast for the latest quarter earlier this month, sending its shares tumbling. And even Apple Inc.’s prized iPhone has seen demand slow.
Tensions with China also could cast a shadow over Arm’s business. In the filing, the company pointed to export restrictions from the US and UK as risks, hindering its ability to sell its Neoverse processor in China.
Arm plans to change its name to “Arm Holdings Plc” before it begins trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ARM. The filing confirms that the IPO’s top four banks will be acting as joint book-running managers of the offering. Bloomberg News has reported that the four will get an equal share of the fees, breaking with standard practice.
In the filing, Arm called itself an “engineering-first company,” with 4,753 of its workers — or about 80% of global employees — focused on research, design and technical innovation. The company said it owns or co-owns about 6,800 issued patents and has approximately 2,700 patent applications pending worldwide.
In the last fiscal year, more than 260 companies were using Arm-based chips, including Amazon, Alphabet Inc., Qualcomm and Advanced Micro Devices Inc. The company has worked with its top 10 customers — measured by royalty revenue — for an average of more than 20 years.
As AI fever has swept the tech industry, companies will need the right chips to run complex software. Arm says that every processor it designs will accelerate the AI and machine learning tech that it helps power. Its processors already run those technologies, and the company has started adding new functionality to make the algorithms run faster.
As part of that push, Arm is working with Alphabet, autonomous driving company Cruise, Mercedes-Benz, Meta and Nvidia to deploy Arm technology that can run AI-based software.
Arm was founded in 1990 as a joint venture between Acorn Computers, Apple and VLSI Technology. It was listed on the London Stock Exchange and Nasdaq from 1998 until 2016, when SoftBank acquired the business for $32 billion.
SoftBank previously attempted to sell Arm to Nvidia in a $40 billion deal, which would have been the largest chip industry takeover. But the purchase faced opposition from regulators and Arm’s own customers, and Nvidia walked away from it last year. SoftBank then embarked on its plan for the IPO.

title: As fight over AI artwork unfolds, judge rejects copyright claim
text:
A federal judge rejected an attempt to copyright an artwork generated by artificial intelligence in a decision last week that provided insight into the broader legal war over authorship and intellectual property.
The case was unique because an inventor named Stephen Thaler listed his computer system as the artwork’s creator, arguing that a copyright should be issued and transferred to him as the machine’s owner. After the U.S. Copyright Office repeatedly rejected his request, Thaler sued the agency’s director.
“Plaintiff can point to no case in which a court has recognized copyright in a work originating with a nonhuman,” Judge Beryl A. Howell of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia wrote in her decision Friday, adding that “we are approaching new frontiers in copyright as artists put AI in their toolbox.”
Similar rules about “human authorship” have been used in deciding who owned a monkey’s selfie. Thaler created the artwork in question — “A Recent Entrance to Paradise,” a lush but pixelated scene of train tracks running through the countryside — in 2012, by asking his generator to produce an image.
Thaler’s lawyer, Ryan Abbott, said he would appeal the ruling and characterized the legal debates as a critical part of the public’s discourse around the recent generative art boom.
“Do we want rules where you can own what comes out of artificial intelligence?” he said. “Or do we want rules that only protect very traditional, human artworks?”
The Copyright Office said in a statement that it “believes the court reached the correct result.”
This year, the agency established an initiative to examine copyright law and policy issues related to artificial intelligence. Around the same time, it released guidance for submitting creations that included AI-generated work, saying that applicants were required to specify human authorship and should explain which portions were produced by an algorithm.
The ruling against Thaler was “significant but not surprising,” said Megan Noh, an art lawyer unaffiliated with the case who said the decision conformed with the office’s guidelines and previous court rulings. She added that it did not mean “other artworks produced with AI assistance will not or cannot be registrable.”
There is an onslaught of upcoming cases challenging the legality of images and texts generated by artificial intelligence. In July, comedian Sarah Silverman joined lawsuits accusing OpenAI and Meta of training their algorithms on her writing without permission. Other companies such as GitHub and Stability AI are facing litigation that accuses them of illegally scraping artists’ work for their AI products.
Jason M. Allen, the artist whose victory last year at the Colorado State Fair’s annual art competition prompted widespread discussion about generative artwork, is pursuing his own case against the Copyright Office.
His request for copyright as the sole author of images produced by a generative algorithm was denied by the agency and he is awaiting its decision on a second appeal. Allen said that he was prepared for a court fight, explaining that artists want control of their work regardless of the tools used to make it.
“You cannot separate the tool from the user,” he said. “By separating the tool from the user, you are dismissing the person who made it.”

title: Russia’s New Long-Range Kamikaze Drone Will Be Built In A Shopping Mall
text:
Russia’s big Army 2023 Expo last week featured the expected flurry of announcements of new kamikaze drone projects. Many of these will be pure vaporware, a category in which Russia has long excelled, but some deserve to be taken more seriously. A new weapon known simply as Izdelie 54 (‘Product 54’) may be significant simply because of who is making it.
A press release from the show gave minimal information:
“AEROSCAN at the international military-technical Forum Army 2023 announced a new model of long-range loitering ammunition with an enlarged warhead – ‘Product 54.’
The product is designed to destroy military equipment and manpower of the enemy, located at a considerable distance.
This model is an initiative development of the company, uses the latest artificial intelligence algorithms and is currently undergoing final tests before being put into production.”
As we have seen, numerous Russian companies are attempting to break into this market, as kamikaze drones or loitering munitions have been among Russia’s few successes during this war. The Lancet, a 25-pound drone with a 7-pound warhead has shown itself capable of knocking out artillery tanks and other armored vehicles from 25 miles away. (The biggest issue seems to be targeting; numerous Lancet kills are actually dummies, and one recent video posted as a ‘success’ seems to show a Lancet destroying a Russian T-90M tank). Meanwhile Russia continues to bombard Ukraine with 450-pound, Iranian-made Shahed-136 kamikaze drones and it attempting to started up a factory to mass-produce a Russian version under license. These drones have a range of several hundred miles.
What makes Product 54 interesting is that it is made by Aeroscan, a company run by Nikita Zakharov, son of Alexander Zakharov, a businessman with a controlling 50.85% interest in Zala Aero Group which makes the Lancet. (The rest of the shares are owned by the Kalashnikov Concern, and Lancet of often referred to as being a Kalashnikov product.
Aeroscan has been very much below the radar, with virtually no information about their projects, they make a reconnaissance drone known as Z-20 but it is not known whether this is in production or service.
It seems highly unlikely that Nikita Zakharov, would go into competition with the family’s main business (Incidentally, he appears to have been to Oxford University and owns luxury real estate in London). In fact It is more probable that the new Product 54 is a long-range drone intended to compete with the Shahed. As we saw previously, the Russian company attempting to make Shaheds may have some difficulty, and with Zakharov family know-how and connections Aeroscan may be able to make up the shortfall and tap a rich vein of procurement cash from Russia’s Ministry of Defence.
And we have a good idea exactly where this business will be based. On December 30 last year, the tenants of the Italmas shopping mall, in the city of Izhevsk 700 miles east of Moscow had their leases terminated. These included a supermarket, several fashion outlets, a pizza parlor and a former McDonalds. A local news investigation found that the mall has been acquired by Aeroscan, apparently for the production of drones. The city is no stranger to the arms business; its biggest tourist attraction is the Kalashnikov Small Arm's Museum Exhibition Complex and by no coincidence it is also Alexander Zakharov’s home town.
In August 2020, Alexander Zakharov suggested that shopping malls selling foreign brands should be shut down and repurposed for drone production. It seems as though he was serious.
This sounds like the set-up for a new Russian reversal joke: “In America you go to shopping mall to get new gadgets. In Russia, new gadgets come from the shopping mall to get you!”
…Except this is deadly serious. But how dangerous is it?
“If this Izdelie 54 is a ‘long-range’ drone, it will probably have to compete more with Shahed, but it all depends on specs,” Samuel Bendett an expert Russian drones and adviser to both the CNA and CNAS, told Forbes. “It's possible that this new drone will fill the gap between Lancet and Shahed capability - with a range of 80-200km, or may be designed for even longer ranges.”
Of interest is the claim that the 54 ‘uses the latest artificial intelligence algorithms’. The Lancet is notable for having a U.S.-made Jetson TX2 processor is optimized for neural networks to giving drones AI capability, and which is believed to help the Lancet to lock on to targets identified by the operator. The new drone may benefit from more recent and powerful smuggled processors, and the AI algorithms may be used either to aid in navigation, targeting or both. Algorithms links to a drones camera can spot landmarks and navigate when GPS is jammed, and machine learning can identify targets without human intervention.
This capability gives a small drone the ability to hit targets with high precision, making it a more dangerous weapon than a cruise missile with a much larger warhead but less reliable guidance. And at tens of thousands of dollars rather than millions, kamikaze drones give Russia a sustainable way to continue the war.
“What this shows is the growing need for a relatively cheap, capable loitering munition in this war,” says Bendett, noting that Russian volunteer organizations like Project Archangel and Oko Design Bureau are also now designing their own loitering munitions with a long range.
Naturally the war of long-range strike drones cuts both ways. And Italmas shopping mall may now be on the target list.

title: Council Post: How 5G Is Empowering Mining Operations
text:
Founder & CEO of Alp Bora & Co., Alp Bora talks about mining, sustainability and corporate culture.
Mining is necessary for providing many of the raw materials that build our world. But how can we better produce the metals we need responsibly and sustainability?
In my travels, I’ve come to find that this industry is critical to many underdeveloped countries and remote communities. One observation I made while visiting mining sites in Africa was the sector’s reliance on human input for data collection and analysis. For instance, operators were counting the number of trucks that come to the crusher. But couldn’t we unlock the potential of such operations by automating these mind-numbing tasks to cameras and sensors and leveraging the operators in more strategic tasks? This change could improve safety by minimizing human exposure to heavy machinery while also boosting productivity and providing valuable points for data collection and analysis.
I believe that 5G technology combined with the power of AI holds the key to a revolution in mining. Let’s take a closer look at the applications and how they can help open new opportunities for automated operations, enhance coverage, reduce latency and increase reliability.
A Data-Driven Future: The Smart Mine
According to McKinsey Senior Expert Mukani Moyo, “Any mining operation today will have in the thousands or hundreds of thousands of sensors capturing data.” The transformational power of data lies in how it’s collected, sorted, analyzed and presented. Technological advances have set the stage for an Internet of Things (IOT) approach to mining, making data interaction more effective.
A number of mining companies have successfully deployed smart mine technology to improve operations, gaining insights related to equipment performance, orebody and stockpile quality; plant operations; spatial and geological data; and environmental performance, all of which are critical to the successful and safe operation of a mine site. For example, one of the world’s largest gold mining companies, Australia’s Newcrest Mining, collects data from over 100,000 sensors at its Cadia Valley gold mine to create digital twins and to build predictive maintenance models. The company’s chief information officer (CIO) estimated that these data initiatives saved the company over $50 million in 2018.
Integrating 5G With Artificial Intelligence
The revolutionary 5G technology, the fifth generation of cellular networks, has the potential to provide speeds up to 100 times faster than its predecessor, 4G. With its faster connectivity speeds, ultra-low latency and expanded bandwidth, 5G is revolutionizing industries and significantly elevating day-to-day experiences. The adoption of 5G technology in the mining industry has been increasing globally, and major companies like Cisco, Hitachi Energy and Huawei are playing key roles in this trend.
Notably, Huawei has recently partnered with Debswana to introduce the world’s first 5G-oriented smart diamond mine project in Botswana. Thanks to these companies implementing standardized data standards and interfaces, “more than 2,700 sets of equipment at the mine are now interconnected using unified data standards, with 170 million pieces of data streamed to the data lake every day.” This wealth of data can then be utilized by numerous digital models of industrial mining equipment as well as data models and services, allowing for seamless sharing and utilization across all mining operations.
I believe a step change for the industry can happen with the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms with 5G. Using AI, this stored data can be turned into insightful information in near-real time. For example, mining companies can use 5G real-time on-site video and AI algorithms to constantly monitor belt conveyors’ states of operation. As a result, real-time alarms could be triggered when safety or quality issues are detected.
Additionally, tech applications like 5G video calls and 5G video stitching combined with AI capabilities can also make mining more intelligent and further improve worker safety and industry productivity. 5G video calls can be used for communication and dispatching in underground operations, keeping the control center informed at any time. Underground surveillance images can be seamlessly stitched using AI to support precise remote control of the mining face and multiparty 5G video calls. And vehicles can be equipped to handle complex vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) communications, enabling onboard computers to autonomously navigate intersections, even when two vehicles approach perpendicularly.
Making The ‘Smart Mine’ A Reality
The main challenge of the mining industry is to unify systems and industry standards. There are thousands of different devices under each mine, generating millions of points of data. Systems from different vendors have their own data systems and hardware, making it difficult for them to collaborate. Moreover, there are no industrywide standards, which are needed for the industry to innovate toward intelligent mining in the future. I believe industry leaders need to support standardized protocols and collaboration between technology providers, as these are important to enabling effortless data sharing between devices, fostering human-machine and machine-machine interconnections, and enhancing ambient awareness.
As an example of what is possible, consider one cutting-edge development introduced by Huawei: an operating system that focuses on streamlining mining operations by unifying device languages and implementing unsupervised inspections, with the goal of facilitating smoother communication between devices of varying sizes. By utilizing standardized protocols, this can enable more effortless data sharing, fostering improved human-machine and machine-machine interconnections.
Consider also how a collaborative effort between MTN, Minetec Smart Mining, Huawei and opencast Phalanndwa Colliery in 2022 has resulted in the establishment of a 5G-connected coal mine operation. This pioneering initiative is described as “a major step toward digital transformation of the coal industry.” As a result, the command and dispatch center can now quickly and effectively identify critical situations (such as gas overflows), coordinate organized evacuations, and promptly initiate shutdown procedures for mining equipment. This improved capability can significantly enhance the efficiency of emergency response operations.
Beyond Safety And Productivity
The integration of 5G technology in mining can enable accurate, real-time data capture and analysis. This approach, when coupled with AI algorithms, may also be able to enhance environmental and social performance, helping to address vital issues like air pollution and water conservation while allowing for remote monitoring of safety-critical elements such as tailings dams. Ultimately, I believe such an integration of data from diverse sources is an important step for mining industry leaders because it can position companies at the intersection of risk management, human factors and data science, empowering decision-makers with accessible and valuable ESG risk information.

title: Council Post: The AI Judge: Should Code Decide Your Fate?
text:
Charles is managing partner of The Lew Firm, Attorney and Entrepreneur who owns and operates multiple hospitality concepts.
A close legal associate of mine often recounts how a benevolent judge granted him probation and a diversion program instead of being tried as an adult with a minimum of five years in prison for his indiscretions as a 17-year-old. He vividly describes the learned face of the judge scrutinizing him from the stand for what seemed like an eternity before delivering a monologue about his hopes that the young man before him would see the error of his ways and that if he did, he would have a bright future. That young man turned into a successful business owner, husband and father, who by all accounts, is a respected and venerable pillar of the community today. What did the judge see that day? What was said by that young man, or perhaps more importantly, what wasn't? What in his face, stance and nonverbal communication allowed the judge to make an incredibly prescient determination that would drastically alter the trajectory of this youth's life?
Three decades later, we stand at a crossroads. AI emerged in 2023 as the most potent technology the legal world has ever seen. Perhaps more startling is the rapidity with which it is improving, prompting at least one expert to use the term "compounding exponential" progress to describe anticipated future advancements. As AI continues its inexorable march forward, the application of AI to the law will undoubtedly increase. Large language models such as ChatGPT see extensive use in the daily practice of law, perhaps even overuse, as lawyers seek shortcuts to repetitive and laborious tasks to the detriment of accuracy and with sometimes calamitous results.
Researchers at Tel Aviv University claim to have created the most accurate lie detection system ever produced. This revolutionary AI technology reads, records and analyses micro-expressions to determine truthfulness and is arguably already more precise than its human counterparts. We then contemplate what the cost for this accuracy, neutrality and objectivity may be. Is it possible to synergize AI's power and predictive analytics with the wisdom of a human jurist?
The legal system is experiencing a metamorphosis on account of the transformative power of AI. Lawyers' broad and expanded utilization of AI is inevitable; the question remains, how long before the judiciary implements AI to assist with their judicial responsibilities? When will our percipient trier of law surrender or, at the very least, share its hallowed seat with a computer? The answer to this query may surprise you. Earlier this year, a Colombian judge utilized ChatGPT (registration required), stating, "The decision is mine—ChatGPT backs up my decision," the judge went as far as itemizing verbatim the prompts he used in ChatGPT to elicit the AI-generated answers even, including the complete responses in his ruling.
This certainly leads me to wonder where my associate would be today if, instead of a sagacious and compassionate judge thirty years ago, he was instead sentenced by a calculating automaton that crunched a prodigious amount of data to arrive at a sentence that, although fair, may have lacked the intangible human qualities of empathy, sensory perception and comprehension of contexts such as cultural, historical and social factors that influence and impact critical decision making. Do we believe that the traditional court system can deliver impartial determinations in the 21st century? Is the complexity of the quandaries facing our citizenry such that AI would not only be welcome for its problem-solving capabilities but as a moral necessity?
While the judiciary will continue to embrace and integrate imminent technological advances, I believe it must do so prudently. Algorithmic equality must be thoroughly and consistently audited and monitored to ensure that the systems designed to expedite justice and prevent unequal and biased treatment do not inadvertently facilitate the implementation of such discriminatory practices. According to a new Harris poll, eight in 10 Americans believe that our court systems can no longer deliver an impartial or non-biased ruling, and slightly more than 40% would trust their fate to an AI judge rather than the more traditional carbon-based trier of law. The Harris poll highlights a grave and growing distrust for the judicial system. While one cannot contemplate AI being a panacea for this general skepticism toward the judiciary's neutrality, I think increased use of AI and machine learning technologies will likely engender a return to a degree of confidence that has been steadily declining.
Assuming a strategic division of labor between our human judge and AI could utilize each party's relative strengths, it begs the question of how to protect against the potential for bias within the AI system. I believe continuous and consistent auditing of the AI system will be required to address ethical considerations and to ensure nondiscrimination. We must concern ourselves not only with the unintentional programming of bias into the system by the programmer but the far more disturbing and insidious nature of swathes of inherently prejudiced but seemingly objective data serving as the source for the progressive learning of the algorithm.

title: Council Post: AI Is Remixing Music—But The DJ Is Still A Human
text:
David Beiner, CEO and Co-Founder of Hume.
As AI goes mainstream, questions have surfaced regarding concern for its implications for musical artists. There has been speculation about its impact on human jobs and whether it could lead to a total loss of our humanity.
The truth is that successful, AI-generated art will still require a human touch. Despite its ability to automate tasks and generate images, AI (for now) is still limited by the abilities and decisions of the people responsible for its creation, editing and programming.
Harmonic Evolution
Collaboration between humans and technology is critical and has always been evolving. Our relationship with technology throughout the creation process will continue to be essential.
When digital audio workstations (DAWs) began to go mainstream in the late ’90s and early 2000s, it fundamentally changed how music was created. The at-home studio and bedroom artist were made possible. The need to pay for expensive recording studios gave way to a generation of artists and songwriters creating hits in their living rooms. At the time, this digitally driven creative process felt extremely different from anything that had come before it.
Around the same time, another new technology, Auto-Tune, literally changed the pitch of artists’ voices. It also allowed artists who previously may not have been considered good singers to sing far better or more uniquely than what they could achieve on their own. It opened the door for artists to create a unique vocal style and leave their own mark on the music industry.
In both cases (and especially in the case of Auto-Tune), a new technology opened the door for completely new areas of creativity, and the marriage of technology and artistry took on new forms.
Today, we’re at a new DAW or Auto-Tune moment, as AI is poised to change the game once again. Will AI innovation open the door for new artists? Yes. Do we know which music genres, artists and styles will ultimately benefit? Not yet. However, we do know new types of music and forms of creativity are on the verge of becoming mainstream.
Using AI—Legally
We’ve seen AI start to make its way into music with Drake’s AI clone and DJ David Guetta using Eminem’s vocals in a set. While these instances garnered tons of attention, they were met with equal criticism regarding copywriting contingencies. There was also a big question as to whether it was appropriate to create models of their voices without their permission.
For this new era to be successful and sustainable, we need to determine a fair, legal framework for AI music—specifically around voice cloning. If the industry can find a balanced way that values innate human talent and the aims of artists who want to blend that talent with AI, we could enter a golden era of music creation.
In that new world, songwriters would be empowered to create music that captures the imaginations of listeners everywhere. Previously impossible collaborations between living and legendary artists could top the charts. DJs could incorporate all sorts of vocalists in their songs. Existing artists could find new avenues to collaborate with others and their fans.
Take Grimes’ AI voice, for example. The avant-garde singer invited creators to use AI-generated versions of her voice to make new music, saying she would “split 50% royalties on any successful AI-generated song” that was released. Her AI project has inspired other artists to use it in their own creations. In this case, AI allowed Grimes to collaborate with her fans and draw on new sources of creativity in a way that was never previously possible.
Remixing Music With AI
Notwithstanding Grimes’ worthy experiment, there’s a misconception that AI-generated music is as simple as clicking a button. Each creative process involves numerous hours of work and people behind the scenes. In most cases, the music is still produced by a producer, and a singer is still recording an actual song. Using AI, those vocals get cloned as someone else’s voice.
The project Grimes launched with her AI voice shows that while AI technology can certainly assist in the music production process, it is still dependent on human creativity and effort to bring it to life. Thousands of human vocalists and songwriters are still writing and creating music but are able to have it sound like Grimes because of this new technology.
While this new framework looks different from traditional songwriting and pitching, you could argue there are now even more opportunities for songwriters to have their work released by major artists and become compensated in new ways.
By leveraging AI tools like ChatGPT as a writing assistant and techniques like cloning a real artist’s vocals, creators can push the boundaries of their craft and explore new possibilities while retaining their unique perspectives and artistic visions. The collaboration process is where human imagination and artistic expression will come to life. In essence, AI is not a substitute for human creativity but rather a tool that can amplify it.
While there are concerns about AI replacing human creativity, the momentum of technology is often unstoppable. In most cases, history has shown us that artists adapt to new technologies and incorporate them into their processes. I believe that if we implement AI with the proper legal frameworks in place, learn to appreciate the human input as well as the new forms of collaboration that are coming, and value the work humans do after the AI has done its job, we will be able to welcome in this new era of creativity more excitedly. It will be an era unto its own.

title: Council Post: Overcoming Fear To Realize The Benefits Of Artificial Intelligence
text:
Wai Wong is the Founder, President and Chief Executive Officer of Serviceaide, a global provider of enterprise service management solutions.
After years of futuristic story plots and prognostications, artificial intelligence (AI) is a technology that appears to be catching up with its hype. Designed to perform and automate cognitive tasks that once required human brainpower, AI has been advancing rapidly of late—in fact, too rapidly for some.
The sound of alarm bells has been jarring at times. Critics, including insiders, have made headlines expressing concerns that AI could cause societal harm by overtaking human intelligence, stealing jobs from knowledge workers and perhaps going rogue as it develops a mind of its own.
In March 2023, a group of some 1,100 technologists and researchers, including Elon Musk, signed an open letter calling for a six-month moratorium on AI development to assess perceived threats. The letter warned of the potential for “non-human minds that might eventually outnumber, outsmart, obsolete and replace us.”
As a long-time technology executive and entrepreneur who's been working for the past seven years to harness the power of AI to drive business value and efficiency, I find these concerns to be premature at best, if not highly overwrought. Instead, I tend to agree with the thoughts of Yann LeCun, one of the three so-called “godfathers of AI,” who argues that we're years and perhaps decades away from AI surpassing the human intellect. Meanwhile, controlling AI will be well within our power. To quote LeCun, “It’s still going to run on a data center somewhere with an off switch. And if you realize it’s not safe, you just don’t build it.” (It should be noted that the other two "godfathers of AI," Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, have expressed concerns about the potential dangers posed by AI.)
Yes, the progress of AI should be followed closely and perhaps subject to ethical regulations over time, but seeking to delay its advancement strikes me as impractical, unnecessary and counterproductive. AI is currently delivering major practical benefits to businesses and society with the potential to do much more. It has the capacity to generate a huge boost in world productivity. Goldman Sachs analysts, for instance, estimate that AI could increase global GDP by 7%, or nearly $7 trillion, and boost productivity growth by 1.5 percentage points over the next 10 years.
AI is helping transform a wide range of industries, business processes and applications. In healthcare and medicine, for example, it’s being used to improve medical care and reduce costs across drug discovery, diagnostics, patient interactions, administrative processes and more. In cybersecurity, it's used to better identify vulnerabilities and threats and respond to attacks. In marketing, it's helping identify behavioral patterns, improve personalization and develop advertising and other marketing content. AI is also being used to write and debug software code to accelerate development.
Recent advances in generative AI have been perhaps the most remarkable development in AI. Generative AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, DALL.E and Bard, utilize pre-established foundational models to train and learn from vast amounts of data without specific intervention and programming from humans. They can adapt to address a broad range of questions and tasks, including creating and editing content, such as text, images and video.
When fine-tuned with an organization’s own data, these AI foundational models can be deployed to effectively perform specific tasks and deliver significant improvements in business processes and outcomes. In service and support, generative AI represents a huge step-change in self-service delivery, often reducing wait times, improving productivity and cutting the cost of support across the full range of IT and other enterprise services. Isn’t this at the heart of digital transformation?
Generative AI can allow service organizations to overcome current limitations in accessing and delivering knowledge and solving problems for users and support groups. Intelligent chatbots or virtual agents and self-service portals can tap into vast repositories of information across the internet to find answers to questions and troubleshoot problems that are entirely new to an organization. Generative AI-powered service and support systems could self-generate accurate, concise summaries from disparate information and content to improve knowledge delivery to users and support personnel.
The result is expected to be more productive enterprises and more cost-efficient and effective service management processes. Rather than stealing jobs from knowledge workers, AI increasingly will more likely empower countless employees to do their jobs better and with less stress and bottlenecks.
The fear of automation and technological advancement has been with us for centuries. The infamous Luddite movement in the early 1800s resulted in workers destroying textile equipment they believed threatened their livelihoods, eliciting violent counterattacks on workers by manufacturers. Technology disruption drives changes in business processes and the roles and opportunities of workers.
AI is undoubtedly a giant next step in this ongoing process of change and disruption. It has known and unknown ramifications for the future of work and our society. For that reason, its development and application need to be monitored closely and perhaps regulated in the years ahead. However, the opportunities for improving business efficiencies and the lives of people everywhere demand that we continue to develop and apply it for good.

title: Council Post: How Firms Can Prepare For The Rise Of AI In Venture Capital
text:
Ali Baghchehsara, general partner at plasmso.vc.
Venture capital (VC), long regarded as the pulsing heart of innovation and entrepreneurial risk-taking, is on the brink of transformative change. When VC industry giants like Mike Moritz from Sequoia step back, it underscores an impending shift in the rhythm of venture capitalism.
Challenges such as inexperienced general partners (GPs) and hurdles in fund-raising have nudged the sector into a period of introspection and self-reinvention. Likewise, technology innovation is impacting VC as much as the companies that VC supports.
Consider AI. Silicon Valley veteran James Currier, general partner at early-stage venture capital firm NFX, offers an insightful and daring view: "AI is going to remake the startup industrial complex, from its core. Venture firms will have to remake themselves into a combination of people and AI." This statement heralds a future where the traditional VC landscape could be radically altered by the integration of AI, data analysis and machine learning.
However, this raises intriguing questions about how AI will disrupt venture capitalism specifically.
The Advent Of AI In Venture Capitalism
AI's relevance in venture capitalism extends beyond its impressive technological prowess. It is intimately tied to the vast datasets it processes and analyzes. VC decision-making—which traditionally involved navigating through pitch decks, conducting in-person meetings and heavily relying on human intuition—could be entirely reshaped by AI.
The current approach, fraught with subjectivity when performed by humans, has many opportunities for automation through AI. Likewise, entrepreneurs could see funding approved quicker, disrupting the foundational structure of the startup ecosystem.
Visualize a future, for example, where pitch decks are superseded by AI-led interviews. The transcriptions from these interactions become raw data that can be processed to objectively and efficiently identify distinct character traits and potential for investment.
The ability of AI to process vast quantities of data swiftly and accurately provides these firms with insights that might be impossible for human analysts to uncover within a comparable timeframe.
Because of this possibility, VC firms are beginning to explore the potential of AI in refining their investment processes. Companies like Correlation Ventures and InReach Ventures are harnessing machine learning to evaluate potential investments based on comprehensive data analysis.
The implications of AI in venture capitalism extend beyond speeding up decision-making processes. AI could be instrumental in introducing a new form of equity distribution. Many tech workers in Silicon Valley are motivated by the desire to engage in meaningful and innovative work, not just to earn significant salaries.
With AI's data-driven system, these passionate individuals could be matched with rising founders working on groundbreaking projects, fostering a synergy that could lead to remarkable innovation.
Confronting Challenges
The potential for AI in VC is clear, but the pathway to an AI-dominated VC industry also features several challenges. For example, here are a few to consider:
Algorithmic Bias
Bias in data and algorithms poses a significant concern as it could lead to inequitable decision-making. AI systems, trained on past data, may inadvertently perpetuate the biases present in those datasets. To ensure a fair and diverse ecosystem, AI systems need to be meticulously audited and trained on unbiased data.
Building Trust
For AI to establish itself in the VC world, it must secure early victories. Like traditional VCs, AI needs to demonstrate its ability to consistently pick winners to gain trust and pave the way for widespread adoption.
The Diminishing Role Of Brand Investors
The increasing integration of AI into venture capitalism could potentially diminish the role of brand investors. This might appear as a disadvantage, but it could inadvertently expedite the adoption of AI in the VC industry.
Power dynamics within the industry are bound to change as technology plays a more significant role, and VC firms need to adapt to thrive in this new reality. That said, AI could also open doors to wider opportunities, connecting investors with projects beyond traditional hubs.
AI And The Future of Employment
The influence of AI on venture capitalism could also significantly impact employment, particularly within the VC industry itself. As AI takes over more traditional VC roles, the demand for human analysts and partners may decrease. However, this shift could also create new jobs focusing on AI system management, data analysis and machine learning. This signifies a shift in job types rather than a decrease in job numbers.
In short, investing in AI-related competencies is a must.
The Future Landscape
The adoption of AI could usher in a global innovation wave. Imagine AI-driven platforms effortlessly linking investors with untapped global opportunities, displacing traditional methods and inaugurating an investment world hitherto unexplored.
AI's emergence in venture capitalism is more than a technological shift; it's a paradigm alteration. While traditional tools like pitch decks may wane in relevance, a more accessible and efficient venture capitalism landscape is unfolding. This transformation, far from merely possible, is vital for the continued democratization and innovation of the industry.
