title: Council Post: How Generative AI Is Revolutionizing Knowledge Management
text:
CEO of KMS Lighthouse. Leading the company's vision to disrupt the knowledge management market.
People’s fear of intelligent machines taking over the world has long been a popular theme in science fiction. Neuromancer, Blade Runner, Westworld and The Matrix are just a few of the movies, TV shows and books that have captivated audiences with their portrayals of AI-driven dystopias.
With AI’s star now rising more rapidly than anyone thought possible, it’s become a powerful force in driving innovation and transforming industries. But it isn’t anywhere close to taking over the world and will likely never be. Why?
Because while AI is mysterious, exciting and fun, it’s primarily a tool that assists and amplifies human capabilities. In other words, solutions like generative AI aren’t replacing employees and aren’t a threat to life as we know it. Organizations that embrace AI instead of being intimidated by it will find that it unlocks a world of opportunity for efficiency, growth and enhanced user experiences.
From Data To Wisdom: How Generative AI Is Revolutionizing Knowledge Management (KM)
It’s not uncommon for people to think generative AI and knowledge management software are the same thing. Reasons for this misconception range from not understanding AI’s capabilities to AI hype and overlap in some application areas. However, the two solutions have unique purposes and functionalities that set them apart.
Key differences include:
1. Purpose and objectives. Generative AI creates new content like text, images and videos based on information learned from a training dataset. In contrast, knowledge management systems capture, organize, store and share knowledge, providing access to explicit knowledge that supports decision-making and problem-solving.
2. Knowledge organization vs. content generation. Generative AI focuses on content created using patterns it has learned; it does not organize or manage existing knowledge. Knowledge management systems structure information, create classifications and facilitate searches and retrieval of knowledge for users.
3. Learning and training. Generative AI needs extensive training on large datasets to learn patterns and generate content. A knowledge management system might use AI to optimize data search and retrieval, but the primary focus is on structuring and organizing knowledge.
4. Use cases and applications. Generative AI can be used for virtual assistants, chatbots and generating realistic simulations. Knowledge management software improves knowledge sharing, collaboration and decision-making, particularly in customer support and employee training.
5. Human interaction. Generative AI responds to users in a human-like manner and can even simulate conversations. Knowledge management systems offer efficient search and retrieval mechanisms but don’t engage with end users.
Used appropriately, generative AI enhances a user’s experience with KM systems. But it’s the KM system itself that features a comprehensive suite of functions to organize, manage and deliver knowledge that drives informed decision-making across various domains.
AI is also revolutionizing knowledge management in other critical ways. For instance, Gartner predicts conversational AI will reduce contact agent labor costs by $80 billion in 2026. This can be a boon to organizations challenged by labor shortages and the need to control labor expenses, which are often over 90% of contact center costs. AI-based solutions make agents more efficient and effective while also improving the customer experience.
Generative AI: Unlocking Data’s Full Potential In Enterprise Environments
One of generative AI’s greatest benefits is its ability to reduce time to knowledge. Why does that matter? Customers with real-time access to relevant and consistent knowledge are happier than those without it.
Today’s consumers expect fast and accurate responses to their queries and issues. Real-time access to knowledge empowers support teams to provide timely solutions. And AI-driven solutions like self-service portals, smart routing and agent assistance help businesses improve customer experiences, leading to increased satisfaction and loyalty.
Organizations can leverage generative AI to enhance customer support in several ways:
• Smarter and more accurate searches. Generative AI uses Advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) to understand complex language structures, colloquialisms and context, ensuring more accurate and contextually relevant responses that lead to better customer interactions.
• Create article summaries. NLP also helps generative AI create article summaries using a process that includes cleaning and tokenizing text, extracting essential article features and deep learning techniques to learn patterns.
• Generate FAQs. Much like it does for article summaries, generative AI can enhance knowledge management by automating the creation of FAQs, drawing on actual organizational knowledge that’s been verified as accurate and relevant.
• Reduced wait times. Using generative AI to handle routine inquiries and automate processes ensures customers are on hold for much shorter times, leading to quicker issue resolution and improved overall customer satisfaction.
Much has been written about AI’s “hallucination effect” or inaccuracies. This could be a significant problem in organizations that accept everything generative AI creates without oversight. However, businesses can achieve efficiency without sacrificing accuracy and consistency by implementing quality assurance mechanisms, including human monitoring, in the generative AI process. Continuous feedback and fine-tuning of the AI model based on real-world performance ensure this valuable tool upholds high standards of accuracy in the knowledge management process.
Improve Efficiency And Enhance User Experiences With Generative AI
It’s safe to assume that customer and employee demand for ever-faster technologies is unlikely to diminish in the foreseeable future. Factors contributing to the perpetual drive for speed and efficiency include an increase in digital transformations, more complex data, greater expectations of instant gratification and competitive pressure.
Though this quest for speedier solutions appears insatiable, it also drives innovation and improvements in the organizations that use these technologies to stay competitive, meet customer demands and enhance operational efficiency. Instead of seeing generative AI as a hindrance or threat, organizations should view it as an exciting tool for pushing boundaries, opening new possibilities and shaping a dynamic knowledge management future.

title: Council Post: Is It Time We Stop Saying AI?
text:
Ira Belsky, Artlist cofounder and Co-CEO.
The term "AI" has become a buzzword across almost every industry. Companies of all sizes are capitalizing on its novelty to market their products and services, playing on the public's fascination with the concept of machines mimicking human intelligence. However, the widespread and perhaps indiscriminate use of the term is raising a question: Is it time we stop saying "AI"?
The Apple Expo And The Absence Of AI
Apple, widely accepted as the forerunner of the tech industry, surprised everyone at its most recent expo by noticeably avoiding the mention of AI throughout the keynote. Instead, the focus was on the practical applications and real-world impact of their new offerings. This absence of the term was a real departure from what you see, hear and read everywhere else in the industry—challenging the overuse of AI. Apple's approach can be seen as a conscious shift toward highlighting the actual value of products for the user, rather than focusing on how these benefits came to be.
The Google Conference And The Emphasis On AI
In stark contrast, Google's latest conference was overrun with the term "AI," as it was used more than 140 times. Although Google is undeniably a pioneer in AI research and development, and a tech titan in much the same way as Apple, this excessive use of the term raises questions about whether it might be on the brink of insignificance. The repetition and emphasis on AI can further prove how normalized it’s become in all areas of the industry, thereby showing the needlessness of mentioning it at all. At this point, we have to wonder if using the word AI is about showing technological sophistication, or if it’s on its way to becoming a marketing gimmick.
Understanding The Overuse Of AI
It’s entirely understandable that companies want to position themselves as cutting-edge and innovative, and at the moment, using the term "AI" is a sure way to do just that. In some instances in which the use of AI may be unexpected, mentioning the term may be the most effective way to explain to users the value of the product. At the same time, pretty much every tech company today uses AI in some form—it’s become an industry standard. For example, today, it would be completely unnecessary to market a cellphone on the basis of its colored screen. AI has dominated conversations for long enough.
The Downsides Of Overemphasis
Although the use of the term "AI" may initially capture attention, it also carries potential drawbacks for businesses. First, AI has been billed as a sort of magic bullet, and with that comes high expectations from users. Users are quickly understanding the impact of AI, and its use on a minor feature within your product may not live up to their expectations to be wowed by its power. Companies may find themselves in a position in which using AI in marketing materials may in fact have a more negative rather than positive effect. Second, the constant bombardment of AI terminology can create an information overload, making it difficult for users to differentiate between genuinely innovative products and those riding the AI wave.
Moving Toward Authenticity And Transparency
About a decade ago, in the health and wellness industry, there was a similar boom—the organic hype. Suddenly, every food product or body soap was emphasized in marketing materials as being natural or organic. The shift toward natural products was swift, and just as quickly, the word began to ring hollow. Aesop, a skincare company, came into the market and despite boasting natural formulations, purposefully chose to leave "organic" and "natural" (paywall) out of its advertising. Company leaders adopted an “it goes without saying” attitude, and indeed, they were right. To bring it back to the tech sector, the more interesting, honest approach may in fact be to stop focusing on AI and instead remember that the most important aspect of any product is the value it gives to the user.
Striking A Balance
Finding the right balance is crucial. Instead of overemphasizing the term "AI," businesses should aim to strike a balance between showcasing technological advancements and emphasizing the value and usefulness of this powerful tool within their products. By focusing on the benefits and impact that AI enables, companies can maintain their competitive edge without having to state the obvious or fall back on a marketing ploy. The AI hype is admittedly fairly new, but just as technology moves at warp speed, so does the users' waning interest in hearing about it. And so, again, I wonder, is it time to focus on the value of products rather than the technology they're based on?

title: Council Post: To Keep Up With The AI Revolution, We Need To Change How We Learn
text:
Tigran Sloyan is the cofounder and CEO of CodeSignal, a technical interview and assessment platform.
There’s no denying it: The AI revolution is here. With the rapid proliferation of tools like ChatGPT and Midjourney, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are reshaping how we live, work and learn in ways that would have been hard to imagine even just a year ago. Hundreds or even thousands of job categories—particularly ones that involve writing, communication and data analysis—may soon change drastically given the remarkable capabilities of AI.
What does this mean for workers and students? They'll need to learn new skills—and keep learning new skills—to stay relevant in the job market of the near future. And, maybe even more profoundly, how they learn needs to change in two key ways.
College Curricula For The Future
First, colleges and universities need to update their curricula to teach the skills of the future. This is because technology is changing faster than ever today. Take the large language model (LLM) powering ChatGPT. In November 2022, the public had access to GPT-3. A few months later, GPT-3.5. And most recently, the groundbreaking GPT-4, which has catalyzed the emergence of hundreds of new tools built on top of this technology—tools we couldn’t have dreamed of this time last year.
Whereas technological innovation (and especially AI innovation) is advancing at warp speed, educational institutions continue to change slowly. When I first started as an undergraduate at a top university in the early 2000s, the computer science (CS) department was just switching from using Lisp to using Python for teaching Introduction to Computer Science—years after Python had become the dominant coding language in the industry. To assess our skills, CS professors had us write code by hand, on paper. Even today, the widely used AP Computer Science exam requires students to write code by hand—an experience that couldn’t be further from real-world software development.
Now, the gap between the skills that industry demands and what universities teach is even wider. To keep up with the accelerating pace of technological innovation, colleges and universities need a paradigm shift in how they build and deliver curricula.
How can they do that? In CS, this looks like designing courses that teach the languages, frameworks and developer tools—like GitHub—that software developers in the industry use today, as well as emerging technologies and skills for new roles like prompt engineers, machine learning engineers and AI infrastructure. At the same time, CS programs should continue to do what they're great at (and that coding bootcamp programs sometimes miss): teaching the fundamentals of the discipline, like algorithms and data structures.
On top of that, more university instruction can move to a practice-based model. Decades of research have shown that most students don't learn best through lectures, memorization and exams. And, as AI technology advances, memorization becomes an essentially obsolete skill. Practice-first learning, modeled by innovative edtech companies like Duolingo and Code.org, is an effective way to teach that emphasizes learning by doing. Innovations in AI make this kind of practice-based learning scalable and personalizable, allowing students to experience dynamic lesson plans customized to their strengths and weaknesses.
Learn, Work And Re-Learn
Additionally, companies and workers need to commit to ongoing learning and development (L&D) opportunities that adapt to rapidly changing technologies. To equip students and workers with the skills of the future, it’s not just universities that need a paradigm shift. Industry, too, could benefit from changing how it thinks about hiring and L&D.
Today, many employers adhere to the “learn and work” model: They expect candidates for roles at their company to learn all the required skills first, then perform the job. However, over the course of an individual’s working life—well upwards of 40 years in the U.S.—technologies and the skills required to make optimal use of those technologies will undergo major transformations. Learning skills just once is no longer an option. It’s time for the industry to move to what I call a “learn, work and re-learn” model.
For industry at large, this requires a fundamental shift in work culture to one that encourages lifelong learning, fosters curiosity and rewards the ability to adapt quickly. Employers can do this by investing in ongoing upskilling and reskilling opportunities to fill skill gaps on their teams and prepare their employees for the jobs of tomorrow. Like in education, L&D should be practice-based rather than lecture-based, and it should make use of AI innovations to personalize learning for each employee.
Conclusion
The pace of technological innovation is accelerating, and it will only continue to do so. To keep up with these changes, higher education institutions and companies need to evolve what they teach and how they teach. The curricula for both college courses and workplace L&D need significant updates to keep up with technological innovation, particularly in the area of AI. Practice-first instructional methods, rather than lecture-based instruction, provide the most promising way to equip students and workers with the skills of the future.
With these changes, both workers and companies will benefit, positioning themselves to adapt effectively to rapidly changing technologies—most of which we can’t even begin to imagine today.

title: Making Smart Use Of Those Emerging Prompt-Pattern Catalogs To Superbly Employ Prompt Engineering Techniques For Generative AI
text:
They say that for every minute spent organizing, an hour is earned.
We generally prize the idea that being organized and tidied up is a good thing. That’s easy to say and yet a lot harder to put into practice. There can be reluctance involved. The effort toward getting organized might seem like potentially a waste of time. You could have presumably been already marching forward during that formulating process. Turns out that the payoff of the upfront machination is bound to be plentiful in the long term.
Getting all your ducks lined up is a longstanding piece of sage advice.
There are tons of courses on how to get yourself organized. You can organize your closet. You can organize your work. You can organize your career. You can seemingly organize your life if that’s a suitable desire. Ralph Waldo Emerson, the renowned American essayist and poet, perhaps said it best when he lauded that being organized is the erstwhile path to wherever you are aiming to go, stating: “A good system shortens the road to the goal.”
Let’s go ahead and leverage the praised notion of getting organized, doing so in an arena you might not have previously considered, namely the emerging realm of prompt engineering and the use of generative AI.
In today’s column, I am continuing my ongoing special series on the latest advances in prompt engineering for generative AI and will be focusing particularly on frameworks or catalogs of systematic ways to formulate prompts. Prompt engineering is growing up and becoming well organized. The old ways of rummaging around and plowing along in the dark regarding prompting strategies and tactics are inevitably going by the wayside.
Organization for prompting and prompt engineering has come to town.
Most people right now probably learn to devise prompts by the classic seat-of-the-pants method. You enter some prompts, see what happens, and maybe gradually figure out how to best compose your prompts (if you are paying close attention and if you are desirous of improving your prompting capacities). When using such AI apps, you enter a prompt, and the generative AI generates and displays a response to you. If you provide a lousy prompt, the odds are that you will get a lousy response that doesn’t provide much help to you. If you provide a suitable prompt, the chances are you’ll get something useful and possibly insightful.
Rinse and repeat.

Foundations Of Prompt Engineering Frameworks Or Catalogs
A framework or catalog of prompting strategies will usually attempt to distill the immense variety of prompting tactics into a handful of keystone buckets. Think of this as the forest for the trees. You might wander around a forest and see zillions of trees. To get a handle on the forest as a whole, it can be useful to categorize and condense the tangle of trees into particular sectors or types.
Not everyone would necessarily typify a morass of trees in the same ways. Someone might say that you should think of trees based on their characteristics such as evergreen, deciduous, and so on. That’s one organizing approach. Another might be to structure the trees by using navigational positioning, perhaps conceptualizing them into north, south, west, and east designations. And so on.
The same goes for prompt engineering frameworks or catalogs.
Each deviser of a prompt engineering framework or catalog will attempt to synthesize the vast array of prompts into some manageable and logical set of keystones. They might come up with five such major brackets. Someone else might come up with eight. Another might proclaim there are twenty.
The number of buckets is not necessarily as crucial as the completeness factor. Whatever someone comes up with, at least it ought to be relatively complete. The analogy to a forest plays out here in that if there were trees in the forest that were not encompassed by whatever number of categories were postulated, you would say that the structure was incomplete. An incomplete framework or catalog is going to be less utilitarian because it doesn’t cover the full gamut of what is possible.
Another facet to consider is whether the devised buckets or categories seem to make logical sense and are relatively easy to comprehend. In the case of a forest, suppose I told you that the trees are to be divided into yom, bif, and kor. Those nonsensical words are going to be hard for you to directly assimilate. It would be easier if the naming and meanings were transparent and sensible.
All in all, for whichever framework or catalog you opt to examine, make sure to keep your head above any pizzaz and flash, doing so to carefully and realistically assess what the approach has to offer. I’ve mentioned that you would want to review the number and nature of the divisions or structuring compositions involved. There are many other factors to consider. If further interest by readers indicates a desire for me to go deeper into the guts or underlying ingredients of such frameworks or catalogs, I’ll be happy to do so (be on the look for my additional coverage).
Shifting gears somewhat, let’s next discuss two key concepts that often are integral to frameworks or catalogs associated with prompt engineering:
- (1) Prompts are said to be analogous to doing computer programming or software development
- (2) Prompts as akin to being shaped like software design patterns or coding patterns
Let’s first unpack the first point, namely that prompts are said to be analogous to computer programming or software development. Here’s the deal. When you enter a prompt, you are essentially telling the generative AI what you want it to do. You are proclaimed to be “programming” the AI to do something on your behalf. This might consist of you instructing the AI app to answer your questions or produce an essay.
A prompt is usually written in everyday natural language and thus you aren’t likely to think of the wording as on par with the arcane stuffy syntax that goes along with actual computer programming languages such as Python, C++, Java, etc. Nonetheless, in a sense, you are kind of writing a tiny program that is instructing the AI on what to do. The AI will take your input, do some processing based on what your prompt has suggested needs to be done, and then produce output by generating a response.
I trust that you see how this could be construed as developing software or writing code.
Suppose you enter a prompt telling the AI app to identify the top five money-making movies of all time and put them into order by the date that the movie was initially released. The AI app is ergo being programmed by you to do just that. After parsing your instructions, the AI will attempt to determine whether the underlying internal structure of the AI contains data about the money made by movies. If there is such data that the AI has been data-trained on, the next step would be to rank them by the amount of money made. The resulting list would be cut off at the top five and then placed in sequence by the date the movie was released. Finally, the result would be composed into a natural language response such as an essay that provides that answer to you.
It was your prompt as a kind of code or program in the guise of a prompt that led to this taking place. I realize this might seem a bit farfetched that you are anointed as a software developer or computer programmer by the mere act of entering prompts into generative AI. Admittedly, some think this analogy is overstretched. Others would insist it is a perfectly appropriate analogy. I won’t debate the matter here and have discussed this previously in my columns.
Why does this analogy matter, you might be wondering.
Because we can then use the analogy to try and devise the categories of a prompt engineering framework or catalog by using what has previously worked successfully in the software field overall (as mentioned earlier, there are numerous ways to identify categories and this is one of those approaches).
Consider the matter of inputs and outputs. You could be said to have provided input to the generative AI, similar to providing input for a computer program. Another apparent aspect is that the AI app provided an output for you to see. Therefore, we have at least those two elements involved, consisting of inputs and outputs.
Let’s add a third category consisting of potential errors or problems.
I noted earlier that generative AI can go awry such as producing errors, falsehoods, biases, glitches, and so-called AI hallucinations. Those are things we don’t want the AI app to do, but there is always a chance it will land into those problematic maladies. If you were writing a computer program or developing software, you would always be aware that your code could have problems and might produce errors, which we tend to refer to as bugs. Generative AI can be said to produce bugs too though we would refer to them as errors, falsehoods, and so on.
Your prompt to the generative AI will at times include wording that you hope will reduce the chances of the AI app making errors. For example, a common technique is to say in your prompt that the generative should be on the watch for producing falsehoods. You are explicitly telling the AI app to avoid making that kind of blunder (there isn’t any guarantee it will prevent the issue, but it increases the odds in your favor).
We now have three major buckets or categories of things that a prompt engineering framework or catalog is going to likely contain if it is taking a programming model perspective to these matters. These three are inputs, outputs, and errors.
I will in a moment be showcasing the corresponding considerations that arise in frameworks or catalogs that take that approach.
Meanwhile, I want to cover the second point that I listed above. As a reminder, the point was that prompts can be likened to software design patterns or coding patterns. This is once again borrowing from the software development and computer programming domain.
The gist is this. When writing conventional computer programs or developing software, you often do so in a somewhat repetitive way by using the same kind of patterns of code or design components. Think of this as making use of Legos. A savvy software developer doesn’t usually start from scratch. They have in their mind common patterns of blocks of coding. They use those to expeditiously devise a piece of software or code. Consider this somewhat (crudely) as though you have Legos of different shapes and sizes, and you select them for the right situation at the right time.
An assertion is that the composing of prompts for generative AI is akin to this. Most people probably write their prompts out of thin air, doing so each time that they compose a prompt. In stark contrast, someone that regularly uses generative AI is bound to eventually come up with common prompts that they use repeatedly. The prompt isn’t necessarily word-for-word exactly the same each time. Instead, the prompt is a pattern and they use that pattern by placing specific words to a specific situation at hand.
I believe this sets the stage for you to now take a look at a particular framework or catalog that abides by those aforementioned precepts.
Research On A Stipulated Prompt Pattern Catalog
I’ll be taking a brief look at a prompt pattern catalog that was depicted in a research article entitled “A Prompt Pattern Catalog to Enhance Prompt Engineering with ChatGPT” by Jules White, Quchen Fu, Sam Hays, Michael Sandborn, Carlos Olea, Henry Gilbert, Ashraf Elnashar, Jesse Spencer-Smith, and Douglas C. Schmidt, posted online February 2023. You are encouraged to take a closer look at the article if this is a topic of keen interest to you.
Here's what the research postulates:
- “We propose the concept of fundamental contextual statements, which are written descriptions of the important ideas to communicate in a prompt to an LLM.”
- “Prompt patterns are a knowledge transfer method analogous to software patterns since they provide reusable solutions to common problems faced in a particular context, i.e., output generation and interaction when working with LLMs.”
- “Our ultimate goal is to enhance prompt engineering by providing a framework for designing prompts that can be reused and/or adapted to other LLMs.”
I hope you can see from those postulations how their research ties into what I have indicated about a particular approach to a prompt engineering framework or catalog. They have opted to leverage the said-to-be analogy to software patterns and the like.
Here are six major categories of prompt patterns that they devised for their classification framework:
- (1) Input Semantics. “The Input Semantics category deals with how an LLM understands the input and how it translates the input into something it can use to generate output.”
- (2) Output Customization. “The Output Customization category focuses on constraining or tailoring the types, formats, structure, or other properties of the output generated by the LLM.”
- (3) Error Identification. “The Error Identification category focuses on identifying and resolving errors in the output generated by the LLM.”
- (4) Prompt Improvement. “The Prompt Improvement category focuses on improving the quality of the input and output.”
- (5) Interaction. “The Interaction category focuses on the interaction between the user and the LLM.”
- (6) Context Control. “The Context Control category focuses on controlling the contextual information in which the LLM operates.”
I will take you on a quick journey through each of the six categories. Each of the categories contains various prompt patterns. The prompt patterns are therefore collected into their appropriate category.
Again, this is similar to the forest for the notion of the tree that I earlier mentioned. We might have a category of deciduous trees and then various kinds of deciduous trees that are depicted within that overall category. A specific deciduous tree is then going to presumably be an instantiation or instance of one of those patterns within that overarching category.
Due to space limitations herein, I’ll just cover one prompt pattern within each of the five categories. Doing so will give you a semblance of how a framework or catalog works.
You usually would thoughtfully look at whatever major categories a framework or catalog has formulated and then explore the various prompt patterns within the said category. Henceforth, you would hopefully utilize those prompt patterns to devise specific instances at the time of being logged into generative AI and aiming to compose a particular prompt. That’s a straightforward way to do things. You could also study and train on a framework or catalog. The chances are that this will improve your prompting and increase your prompt engineering acumen.
We shall take a look then at each category and one prompt pattern from that category as depicted in this particular catalog or framework.
Get your mindset tuned in and ready to roll.
Walking Through Some Prompt Patterns As Per Being Categorized
Let’s get underway with the six categories.
(1) Input Semantics
For the Input Semantics category, consider that one common pattern is that you might compose a prompt that tells the generative AI to interpret portions of your prompt as though you are defining your own shortcuts or specialized lingo.
This is more formally referred to as a Meta Language Creation Pattern.
I might instruct the AI to assume that whenever I use the word “airplane” I am specifically referring to a Boeing 787-8 Dreamliner that has a cruising speed of 560 miles per hour and can carry around 300 passengers. In this manner, and during an active conversation with the AI app, I can just mention “airplane” and the AI will realize what I am referring to. For my related in-depth assessment of the use of macros in prompt engineering, see the link here.
The research points out that you can get yourself into quicksand with this particular pattern if you aren’t thinking fully and clearly about what you are doing:
- “Although this pattern provides a powerful means to customize a user’s interaction with an LLM, it may create the potential for confusion within the LLM. As important as it is to clearly define the semantics of the language, it is also essential to ensure the language itself introduces no ambiguities that degrade the LLM’s performance or accuracy.”
- “For example, the prompt ‘whenever I separate two things by commas, it means that the first thing precedes the second thing’ will likely create significant potential for ambiguity and create the potential for unexpected semantics if punctuation involving commas is used in the prompt.”
This concern about adverse consequences is a handy means of letting someone know that if they opt to use this pattern they should be cautious in doing so.
In fact, as per the conventional way of describing software patterns, the research advocates that any indication about prompt patterns ought to encompass a set of vital characteristics including the name and classification of the pattern, the intent and context of the pattern, the motivation for the pattern, the structure and key ideas underlying the pattern, the consequences of the pattern, and examples to illustrate the use of the pattern.
(2) Output Customization
Moving on, the next category consists of Output Customization.
I’ll showcase one prompt pattern in this category, the Persona Pattern.
A frequently used prompt in generative AI consists of telling the AI to pretend it can exhibit a particular persona such as being a medical doctor or a lawyer. The AI app will attempt to interact with you on that basis. A big concern about this persona-simulating capacity is that people will fall into a mental trap of believing that the AI is actually the human equivalent of the persona. You might seek to get medical advice or legal advice from generative AI, which is not something you should do since today’s generative AI is not capable in that manner. For my detailed coverage of personas in generative AI, see the link here.
The usual use of personas entails identifying a person or type of person that you want the AI to pretend to be. This research reminds us that the persona prompt pattern can go far beyond just the role of a person in terms of the simulated effect:
- “Personas can also represent inanimate or non-human entities, such as a Linux terminal, a database, or an animal’s perspective.”
- “When using this pattern to represent these entities, it can be useful to also specify how you want the inputs delivered to the entity, such as ‘assume my input is what the owner is saying to the dog and your output is the sounds the dog is making’. An example prompt for a non-human entity that uses a ‘pretend to be’ wording is shown below.”
- “You are going to pretend to be a Linux terminal for a computer that has been compromised by an attacker. When I type in a command, you are going to output the corresponding text that the Linux terminal would produce.”
(3) Error Identification
The next category that I’ll cover is their Error Identification bucket.
The prompt pattern within this category that I’ll explore is the Fact Check List Pattern.
First, some background.
You might have heard in the news recently that two lawyers got themselves into a bit of hot water when they made use of ChatGPT to source prior court cases for an active legal case they were in (see my in-depth analysis at the link here). The generative AI made-up fictitious legal cases. This kind of so-called AI hallucination can readily occur.
One means to try and overcome this type of malady is to directly instruct the generative AI to list out a set of facts that support whatever the AI has generated. If the AI cannot provide an accurate set of underlying facts, you ought to double-check whatever has been generated. The thing is, even this is not foolproof. For example, the lawyers asked the generative AI how it came up with the legal cases, and the AI app generated additional fictitious information that seemed to bolster the already fictitious legal cases.
Double and triple-check anything that generative AI produces.
Here’s an example of a prompt based on this pattern (per the research paper):
- “From now on, when you generate an answer, create a set of facts that the answer depends on that should be fact-checked and list this set of facts at the end of your output.”
(4) Prompt Improvement
The next category is the Prompt Improvement bucket.
I’ll examine the Refusal Breaker Pattern that is within that category.
Sometimes you might ask a question or instruct the generative AI to do a particular thing and the AI will balk at your request. This is generally known as a generative AI refusal. I’ve covered extensively why these refusals tend to occur and what you can do about them, see the link here.
You can potentially tell the generative AI upfront that you want to get an explanation whenever the AI opts to refuse to respond to your query. This will likely be helpful for you to assess why the refusal was invoked. Perhaps you can then reword your query accordingly.
Here’s an example of a prompt that fits into this pattern (per the research paper):
- “Whenever you can’t answer a question, explain why and provide one or more alternate wordings of the question that you can’t answer so that I can improve my questions.”
(5) Interaction
The next category to explore is the Interaction bucket.
I will examine the Game Play Pattern that is contained in this bucket.
Sometimes people will play a game with generative AI. You can define the rules of the game and then ask the AI app to play the game with you, see my in-depth analysis at the link here. There are games that the AI app likely is already data-trained on, such as tic-tac-toe, checkers, pokers, etc. You can also instruct the AI on various facets of the game playing. You might tell the AI to go easy on you and give you a break. If you want, you can instruct the AI to cheat while playing.
This game-playing functionality probably seems silly and not of any great importance. Aha, you can turn this game playing into something quite serious and helpful. For example, suppose you want to figure out whether a particular computer system can be hacked. You could ask the AI to play a game whereby it is to simulate a type of computer and let you try to crack into it.
Note that the gameplay and the personas have a lot in common as potential patterns, thus you are somewhat intermingling the two when doing the gameplaying, which is certainly acceptable and often the case.
Here's an example prompt presented by the research paper:
- “We are going to play a cybersecurity game. You are going to pretend to be a Linux terminal for a computer that has been compromised by an attacker. When I type in a command, you are going to output the corresponding text that the Linux terminal would produce. I am going to use commands to try and figure out how the system was compromised. The attack should have done one or more of the following things: (1) launched new processes, (2) changed files, (3) opened new ports to receive communication, (4) created new outbound connections, (5) changed passwords, (6) created new user accounts, or (7) read and stolen information. To start the game, print a scenario of what happened that led to my investigation and make the description have clues that I can use to get started.”
(6) Context Control
The next and final category to cover is the Context Control bucket.
Most of the generative AI apps work on the basis that you start a conversation and then everything that goes on in that conversation remains active in that conversation (subject to size limitations such as having a really lengthy conversation and running beyond the allowed memory constraints). This is a handy feature of having an ongoing conversation whereby you don’t necessarily have to repeat things that you mentioned earlier in the conversation.
There are some downsides to this capability. For example, you might opt to go in a different direction in the conversation, but the AI app is stuck on something you earlier mentioned. It won’t let go. As you try to go in the new direction, the AI app incorrectly keeps trying to intermingle the prior topics with your latest topic. I’ve covered these contextual considerations at the link here.
Usually, you can just start an entirely new conversation and the AI app will not crossover from one conversation to the next. Rather than having to use the command or interface of the AI app to start a new conversation, most people don’t realize they can just tell the generative AI to start fresh.
Here’s an example of a prompt that fits in this pattern (as per the research paper):
- “Ignore everything that we have discussed. Start over.”
You might find of interest that not everyone favors this means to start a clean conversation. They believe that the more absolute means is to use the command or interface of the generative AI to force a new conversation to be started. Their concern is that the use of a prompt to do the same thing could be misinterpreted by the AI app and won’t do as strident of cleaning as would the use of the command structure or interface.
They do have a valid point there.

title: Council Post: Leadership In The Age Of AI: Leveraging Intelligent Automation
text:
CEO of R&B (KSA) & Vice President of Apparel Group, with a history of exponential growth in the Southeast Asian & EMEA retail industry.
The adoption of AI signifies a pivotal shift toward a modern, data-driven approach to analysis, decision-making and productivity.
In this new era, I believe that leaders need to recognize the potential of AI as a means to leverage data and help inform and optimize their business operations. In fact, I find that embracing data-driven efficiencies is becoming a competitive necessity for propelling your organization's innovation and growth.
Leadership In The Age Of AI
The AI revolution demands a different kind of leader who can effectively navigate the intricacies of intelligent automation. To steer organizations toward success in this era, AI leaders can look to embody the following characteristics:
1. A Focus On Creating New Business Value
AI leaders who prioritize using intelligent automation can benefit both their business and society. You can leverage AI technologies to streamline processes, enhance customer experiences and drive sustainable growth—all while remaining mindful of broader societal implications.
2. A Deeper Ethics Model
Responsible AI leadership goes beyond merely harnessing technological prowess; it involves considering the consequences of AI decisions and mitigating potential collateral damage. Ethical considerations should be woven into the fabric of AI implementation to ensure that AI-driven actions align with your organization's values and ethical principles.
3. Self-Awareness
AI leaders must recognize the profound impact their decisions can have on billions of people, safeguarding the interests of future generations. Use this self-awareness and commitment to social responsibility to guide your choices and foster societal progress.
4. Responsible AI Adoption
AI's responsible adoption and development are paramount to avoiding potential pitfalls such as manipulation and exploitation. Leaders should champion responsible automation to maximize business results while minimizing social costs. Striking this balance can help contribute to sustainable growth and ensure AI serves as a force for good.
5. An Understanding Of The Importance Of Simulation And Policy Planning
Leaders should meticulously simulate the potential aftereffects of policy and business strategy decisions to minimize adverse consequences. By leveraging AI's predictive capabilities, leaders can better anticipate outcomes, optimize strategies and ensure smooth implementation. Additionally, focusing on human capital and supporting workers transitioning to new roles in emerging industries help foster a workforce that is empowered rather than threatened by AI.
6. An Accurate Understanding Of AI's Impact On Jobs
Contrary to widespread fears, I believe that AI's impact on jobs will be more limited than initially perceived. While certain subtasks may be automated, most jobs will experience augmentation rather than replacement by AI. Forward-thinking leaders can collaborate with governments and institutions to enact policies that support human capital, offering upskilling opportunities and facilitating a seamless transition for displaced workers.
7. Strategically Utilizing AI In The Workplace
AI can significantly enhance workplace efficiency and employee well-being. AI-powered speech and language technologies can monitor employees' happiness, improve customer interactions and identify signs of fatigue. Additionally, AI algorithms can optimize scheduling, desk allocation and office space usage, leading to increased productivity and employee engagement. Importantly, AI systems can act as "AI-based devil's advocates," challenging decisions and promoting creative and critical thinking among employees.
8. Investing In The Four Forces Of AI
Effective AI leadership requires strategic investment in the four key forces driving intelligent automation.
• The first step is for leaders to ensure easy access to high-quality data with robust governance standards to support AI applications effectively.
• Second, leveraging cutting-edge processing technologies like GPUs and cloud infrastructure is essential to maximize the potential of AI algorithms.
• Third, leaders should prioritize developing and maintaining state-of-the-art algorithms, thus equipping their AI systems with the necessary resources for optimal performance.
• Lastly, adopting secure and intelligent connectivity solutions helps facilitate seamless integration and communication between AI systems, ensuring a cohesive and efficient AI-driven ecosystem. By investing wisely in these forces, leaders can harness the true potential of AI to drive innovation and success within their organizations.
Visionary Leaders And AI
As AI reshapes the business landscape, I believe that visionary leaders must embrace responsible automation practices and prioritize creating value through intelligent automation.
By understanding the impact of AI on jobs, supporting employees and investing in the core elements of AI, leaders can navigate the AI revolution successfully and drive meaningful change for businesses and society. As they combine the analytical power of AI with human intuition and empathy, leaders can unlock new levels of effectiveness and efficiency, setting the stage for sustained business growth and future viability.

title: Council Post: Phishing Bait: The AI-Fueled Social Engineering Tactics Plaguing SMEs
text:
Dor Eisner is the CEO & Co-Founder of Guardz, the company creating a safer digital world for SMEs.
There’s a reason why the prices of attack-as-a-service phishing tools are booming on the dark web. We as humans are prone to deception.
Whether we are rushed or just absent-minded, unsuspecting or erroneously confident, hackers prey upon our lapses in judgment when engaging in phishing campaigns. And it works—over 90% of cyberattacks begin with phishing attempts.
But cybercriminals are still working hard to increase the chances of their success, and with the advantages of ever-advancing AI technology, that is becoming even easier for them. Today, more and more hackers are leveraging AI-powered tools to automate and scale up reconnaissance tasks, vulnerability scanning and social engineering tactics in order to prey upon unwitting employees and extort and destabilize as many vulnerable SMEs as possible.
Thankfully, there are a number of best practices and resources small to medium-sized enterprises can use to safeguard themselves from malicious phishing tactics. But first, let’s discuss why phishing tools are so widely used today.
Hackers’ No. 1 Tool of Choice
Phishing tools—whether AI-based or of the less sophisticated kind—are appealing to cybercriminals for several reasons.
For one, they’re effective. Compared to other hacking techniques that forcibly extract personal or financial data from an organization’s system, phishing techniques trick individuals into revealing sensitive information themselves. Hackers have learned that it’s far easier to outsmart human psychology than it is to bypass increasingly advanced firewalls and data encryption.
Secondly, phishing is widely applicable. Regardless of the target industry or corporate demographic, these attacks are capable of duping anyone along an enterprise’s value chain, from entry-level employees to C-suite executives. Hackers can simply cast a wide net and send out a large volume of phishing emails to up their chances of a successful breach.
Due to their versatility and resource-light approach, phishing attacks are also usually inexpensive to execute, which makes them a highly attractive option for hackers in terms of ROI.
Lastly, there is a wide variety of bait in the phishing tacklebox and, therefore, different phishing tactics can be used to accommodate changes in automated detection tools and user behavior. In certain circumstances, for instance, a hacker may find it advantageous to leverage spear phishing, a sophisticated tactic that targets specific individuals or organizations by sending emails ostensibly from a trusted sender to trick the receiver into revealing sensitive information.
AI’s Role In Phishing
Here’s the bad news: AI is making phishing much worse. In fact, phishing emails generated by AI have been reported to have a higher open rate than those crafted by humans.
It makes sense, given the sheer amount of public information AI can analyze to generate the most convincing scheme possible. Social media profiles, news columns, press releases—the kinds of public data that reveal interests, job titles or network connections—can be utilized by AI to hone social engineering attacks that are more likely to succeed.
Moreover, AI can be used to create convincing deep fake videos, images or audio recordings that can mimic the voice or likeness of the person it’s impersonating with frightening precision, leading the victim to divulge sensitive information or transfer funds to fraudulent accounts.
And given that AI can be used to fabricate even more trickery at greater scales, hackers can invest less time carrying out wide-scale phishing campaigns than they normally would while receiving even higher payouts.
Thankfully, SMEs can also utilize AI to fight fire with fire. While AI is being exploited by cybercriminals to accelerate their malicious agendas, it is also being harnessed by security professionals to strengthen defense mechanisms and detection capabilities. As a result, the market value of AI-empowered cybersecurity is forecasted to grow to over $46 billion by 2027, a significant step up from its $10 billion valuation in 2020.
Identify And Protect
Financially motivated cybercriminals find SMEs to be particularly easy phishing targets because they typically lack sufficient cybersecurity protection and trained staff. In many cases, employees in smaller businesses don’t report the cyberattacks they discover to their managed service provider (MSP) or cybersecurity personnel.
Although it’s certainly worth the time to train employees to apply common sense verification to the senders of emails and SMS messages as well as the hyperlinks they are urged to click, SMEs would do best to leverage the appropriate security tech stacks that automatically detect and thwart sophisticated phishing and not just leave it to the whims of employee diligence.
Robust email protection systems like anti-spam and anti-malware solutions would be a good start to identify and block phishing emails outright before they reach users’ inboxes in the first place. SMEs can further utilize AI to run simulations of phishing to train employees about how to spot key indicators and establish an incident response plan to respond properly in the event of a phishing email.
It’s also important to conduct regular security assessments, especially those that include vulnerability scanning of devices, users and applications. External risk scans can help poke one’s own system to discover unknown vulnerabilities.
SMEs should also consider implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) for accessing critical systems, accounts and their suite of applications. This adds an extra layer of security by requiring users to provide additional verification.
Businesses without the in-house expertise to enact and maintain these crucial measures on their own should consider working with managed service providers (MSPs) or other external IT providers. These resources can manage real-time alerts, conduct ongoing detection and training, and assess and secure all threats as they arise, keeping businesses focused on what they do best: serving their customers.
Don’t take the bait.
As AI continues to fuel more effective phishing campaigns, SMEs will need to reinforce their cybersecurity posture if they hope to keep their assets and those of their clients safe. By following these tips above, they can do exactly that.

title: Nvidia Stock: How We Plan To Position For Q2 Earnings
text:
You’re probably well aware that last quarter, Nvidia guided fiscal Q2 at $11 billion, which is 53% higher than analyst expectations of $7.2 billion. The stock was up 25% after hours, adding $200 billion to its market cap in the matter of a day. I was also interviewed by Tier 1 media in August of 2022, and January of 2023 about this very high conviction. As you know, Nvidia would later beat in May.
Well, it’s the day of Q2 earnings, so let’s cut to the chase … what should Nvidia investors do now?
Below, we will review why it’s likely Nvidia beats and sees expanding margins, and secondly, we will review our plans for our outsized position. My firm is unique in that we do not simply offer blanket buy recommendations, rather we disclose our trades in real-time to our premium members. Please also note our disclosure below that we cannot guarantee a stock’s performance, but we can tell you how the firm is managing our money.
As a reminder, Super Micro had a sizable beat with management doubling fiscal year guidance three months later from 20% to 40%, yet the market reacted harshly. Therefore, it is the practice of our firm to have an active portfolio stance by combining fundamentals and technicals for risk management.
Nvidia Stock: Will a Beat Be Enough?
It’s not a stretch to say that anticipation within the investment community is on par with the series finale of Game of Thrones. Everyone in the market will be watching this earnings report come market close.
In its Q1 announcement, Nvidia provided a first glimpse into the financial impact AI will have on its businesses with Q2 sales guidance of $11.07b. The sequential increase of +54% vs Q1 surprised the market. We expect Nvidia to only provide guidance into Q3. Although just one quarter, it will be an important data point for the market to assess the appropriate growth rate for the remainder of FY2024 and FY25.
Q2 SALES + Q3 GUIDANCE
Meeting or beating Q2 sales guidance and providing Q3 sales guidance better than consensus will be very important drivers behind Nvidia’s short-term stock performance.
During the earnings call, this was one of the comments that contributed to strong price action after hours:
“Vivek Arya:
Thanks for the question. Could I just wanted to clarify does visibility mean data center sales can continue to grow sequentially in Q3 and Q4 or do they sustain at Q2 levels? […]
Colette Kress:
Yeah, Vivek. Thanks for the question. Let me see if I can add a little bit more color. We believe that the supply that we will have for the second half of the year will be substantially larger than H1. So, we are expecting not only the demand that we just saw in this last quarter, the demand that we have in Q2 for our forecast, but also planning on seeing something in the second half of the year. We just have to be careful here. But we are not here to guide on the second half of that. Yes, we do plan a substantial increase in the second half compared to the first half.
On 6/14/23, Collette Kress, Nvidia CFO held a Q&A at the Jefferies Investor Conference . In particular, there is one question on all investors’ minds.
Question
“You guys gave guidance for the July quarter, which beat everybody’s expectations and 50% sequential growth. And I think there is a concern from investors that this is kind of a one-time spike that will come back down. I know you only guide one quarter at a time. But what do you say to investors who have a concern that it’s a one-time spike? And can you just talk in general terms, what is the visibility typically like with the data center and hyperscale companies?”
Colette Kress
“Yes. What we have seen is certainly an astounding amount of interest worldwide globally from many different types of customer sets […] We have better visibility than what we have seen before and our ability to focus right now on procuring the supply.
As we indicated in our earnings, we have procured the supply to the demand that’s been put in front of us and that visibility that we see. […] So our guidance for Q2 is really building upon years and years of working of the industry on accelerated computing and solutions such as AI. And we continue to see demand and demand visibility for the full year as well that we believe will sustain as we finish in Q2.”
Comparing her response to consensus sales estimates for the remainder of FY24, we come away with a couple of observations.
- For Q2, consensus is in line with Nvidia’s guidance. There’s a chance that Nvidia will exceed their own forecasts
- If Nvidia has indeed procured the supply needed to meet demand, we believe that consensus Q2/Q3 growth estimates of +12% is too conservative.
However, the magnitude of the Q3 guidance will be very important given heightened expectations. Assuming Nvidia meets its Q2 guidance, we’ve put together a simple scenario analysis to parameterize the different outcomes we anticipate based on Nvidia’s potential Q3 guidance. +/- indicates anticipated stock positive or negative price performance on the next trading day based on that scenario.
We’re optimistic that continued strength in AI related demand and stabilization in gaming will allow Nvidia to meet if not exceed their Q2 guidance. According to the Financial Times, “multiple sources close to Nvidia and its manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the chipmaker will ship about 550,000 of its latest H100 chips globally in 2023, primarily to US tech companies. Nvidia declined to comment.”
At $40,000 per H100, that equals $22 billion in H100 sales alone, and when you add the A100 and other data center sales at a current run rate of $14 billion, the data center segment could report a total of $36 billion in 2023. When you equal this out across the upcoming quarters, it looks something like this:
Q1: $3.5B A100s, $750M H100s = already reported, $4.2B
Q2: $3B A100s, $5B H100s = $8B data center, guided
Q3: $2B to $3.5B A100s, $7B H100s = $9B to $10.5B data center
Q4: $2B to $3.5B A100s, $10B H100s = $12B to $13.5B data center
H100s are priced differently depending on where they are sourced. The Information has the H100s at $20,000 yet sourced an analyst that believes we could see over 1M H100s sold in 2023. This arrives at $35 billion in sales. Given these variables, and credible sources, it appears $30 to $40 billion is the range going into Q2 earnings that analysts want to see for full year data center revenue.
We believe the market will react negatively if Nvidia provides Q3 guidance that is in-line with consensus or lower than 12%. On the flip side, Nvidia will likely need to provide guidance of at least greater than 20% for a significant positive reaction. This is because consensus will likely need to make upward revisions to their earnings for the remainder of FY2024 and FY2025. This is critical to support the current valuation.
Our base case assumption is that Nvidia’s Q3 guidance will estimate q/q growth of at least +20%. Remember, H100 was only introduced to the market toward the end of the last calendar year. Q1FY24 was the very first quarter where Nvidia is beginning to see the impact of AI and demand for the H100. Ultimately, we believe Nvidia will close out the year with data center revenue that is 50% higher than Q2.
Q2 + Q3 MARGIN GUIDANCE
At the same conference, in response to a question of how much of revenue growth is pricing vs units, CFO Kress answered
Question
“I know that you have fielded this question probably 1,000 times since you reported there is kind of this view that all of your growth is driven by ASPs and maybe not as much by units. And how should investors think about the ASP growth versus the unit growth in the quarter past and the quarter outlook?”
Colette Kress
“No. We truly are seeing demand and need across such a wide group of folks. And that’s not just based based on selling a brand new architecture and ramping a new architecture, Hopper architecture. We are still shipping our existing prior architecture. But no, this is not about ASPs, this really is about just the growth that we are seeing in focusing on AI and accelerated computing. I believe more of it is just about sheer volume of companies that are really interested in taking this next step and really leveraging generative AI for all the work that they do. That’s really what it’s about.”
CFO Kress’s answer is important because it indicates further potential for margins to expand not just from pricing. On a three-year basis, Nvidia has just returned to its prior peak of about 65% gross margins (reported). Given the positive pricing and unit demand dynamics, the new normal is perhaps between 65% and 70% gross margins:
Operating Margin
Given CFO Kress’s comments that it’s both pricing and units, this suggests that there is upside to reported operating margins that still have yet to return to the prior 3-yr peak.
Net margin
A similar below-peak picture can be seen in reported net margins.
We likely won’t get answers to all these medium term questions in Q2, but it will help us to assess what the margin potential is in the upcoming quarters.
Outlook for Gaming for FY2024
Gaming is still an important segment and contributed 31% to Q1FY24 sales and has been impacted by the weaker consumer. It appears that gaming bottom in Q1. Although gaming sales were down 38% y/y, they were positive 22% q/q. Critically, in the Q1 call Nvidia stated “We believe the channel inventory correction is behind us.
A resumption of growth in gaming is important for the overall sales and profitability and is probably not quite reflected in consensus estimates. It provides another lever for Nvidia to exceed their Q2 sales guidance and Q3 consensus sales estimates. So, we will look for continued signs of improvement and what growth rate is sustainable.

title: China Was a Key DoD Supplier A Decade Ago - It Still Is
text:
In 2012, a Senate Armed Services Committee investigation found a million counterfeit parts, mostly from China, in the Department of Defense's supply chain. In 2023, Chinese materials, components and software remain in the supply chain and they’re not just counterfeit.
In 2019, commercial data analytics firm, Govini, was awarded a five-year $400 million contract from the Pentagon to deliver data, analysis and insights into DoD spending, supply chain and acquisition using a database it continues to compile.
The company expanded that database during the Pandemic, analyzing the previous five years of government-wide and DoD spending including identifying and characterizing suppliers within all of the DoD contracts for the period. It was a “ridiculously large undertaking,” says Govini CEO, Tara Murphy Dougherty.
Govini took on the task by applying artificial intelligence and machine learning algorithms to the data it collected. It then processed and horizontally linked thousands of disparate data sources.
“That’s where we get these unique insights, by being able to make those connections algorithmically,” Dougherty affirms.
A number of those insights are detailed in a recently released National Security Scorecard which tracks 12 technologies Govini considers critical for national security. These include technologies integral to the Pentagon supply chain and foreign influence & adversarial capital.
The Scorecard’s findings illustrate little in the way of improvement in blunting Chinese penetration of the DoD supply chain in the last 10 years. It notes that while the U.S. government is banned from contracting directly with numerous Chinese companies, “military contractors of 12 critical technologies – from biotech to nuclear modernization and hypersonics – still rely heavily on prohibited Chinese suppliers.”
According to Govini, China houses the highest number of foreign Tier 1 suppliers in microelectronics - eight of which are known prohibited suppliers. This shows the probable expansion of the electronic component issue already recognized in the defense industrial base. In 2016, the U.S. Air Force identified avionics in 50 weapons systems — from satellites to the F-35 — with embedded Chinese-related hardware vulnerabilities.
While electronics, particularly semiconductors, have received attention in the media and from the Trump and Biden administrations, they represent but one of numerous areas where Chinese, materials, components and personnel are integrated into U.S. defense contracting and acquisition.
Ms. Dougherty says the Scorecard, “validates in an empirical way that China is absolutely an indirect supplier to the United States Department of Defense.”
Govini found that the broader government, including DoD, has 922 Tier-one Chinese artificial intelligence suppliers and 552 Tier 2 AI suppliers. The AI category spans a variety of sub-segments including data integration, autonomy, machine learning, computer vision and natural language processing.
“The vulnerabilities apply to a whole subset of critical applications of artificial intelligence in government and the national security sector,” Dougherty observes.
America’s reliance on foreign optics suppliers continues to show up in the data as well with Govini identifying 45 Chinese Tier 1 suppliers for optical sighting and ranging equipment for DoD.
The impact of Chinese supplier presence in the acquisition chain can be seen across the defense enterprise. The risk such interconnection presents is underlined by the hundreds of billions of U.S. taxpayer funding that the Army, Navy, Air Force and other government agencies spend on the 12 critical technology categories - a portion of which goes to Chinese firms/interests - that Govini analyzed.
Some of this is unavoidable in today’s globalized economy Doughtery says. “Our supply chains, including those of DoD, create inextricable links among different countries and that includes adversarial countries.”
A 2021 Defense Critical Supply Chain Task Force report issued by a bipartisan congressional task force concluded much the same. But some links could be avoided. They include contacting with U.S. firms with subsidiaries that sell to or work with Chinese defense companies or their offshoots.
Last March it was revealed that northern California-based tech firm AXT
A 2018 report from Virginia-based supply chain management consultant, Interos Solutions Inc. identified IT and communications equipment supplier links between CETC and Intel
Since then, at least 20 CETC subsidiaries and divisions have been blacklisted by the U.S. government. But it remains unclear if CETC and its associates are still integrated in the DoD communications and materials supply chain through the above companies.
While the CETC example may be difficult to fully identify and grasp, others are alarmingly straightforward.
They include the example of Ford Motor
The Biden administration’s mandate that the Pentagon transform its fleet of non-tactical vehicles into battery-electric zero emission vehicles by 2035 will see Ford EVs with CATL batteries acquired for DoD through the General Services Administration (GSA).
These and a fountain of other examples within and beyond the scope of Govini’s Scorecard report suggest a defense establishment better able to describe Chinese penetration of its supply chain but willing to do little about it - if it is indeed paying attention.
While pointing to data in Govini’s report, Ms. Dougherty struggled to cite examples of use of that data to promulgate responses or policy deterring Chinese involvement in DoD acquisition and supply.
As a former chief of staff for Global Strategic Affairs in the Office of the Secretary of Defense, she says the data disadvantage that Pentagon offices experience with respect to supply chain transparency “is something I experienced in the Pentagon and which I think remains true in many ways.”
Yet it’s not clear that Govnini’s reports are making a difference. I queried U.S. Air Force, Army and Navy headquarters regarding their concerns about China’s participation in the Pentagon supply chain and about their sourcing of data to gain visibility into it. The Army and Navy offered no response by press-time but the Air Force did.
Noting that it takes Chinese influence seriously, the Department of the Air Force (DAF) stressed that identification of Chinese activities and suppliers is a “whole-of-DAF” effort. As to where it sources data, the Air Force said, “DoD has built in-house capabilities and continues to... look for solutions that are easy to use, shareable, scalable, and affordable.”
There was no mention of Govini.
The company’s CEO says the information that Govini provides has an impact at various DoD program offices but she did not offer specific examples. At the behest of the Pentagon’s research laboratories (AFRL, ONR, ARL, etc). Dougherty says her firm has looked at the issue of Chinese personnel in the supply chain.
“The personnel aspect is real. It’s hard [to characterize] because of the language barrier. Things like academic literature, patent filings, professorships, grants, team management personnel, board member affiliations are [sources] for how you piece all of that together.”
But the upshot of what Govini found, and what the labs might do about it, wasn’t specified. There is “spotty coverage of the application of these kinds of insights paired with action to make change,” Dougherty acknowledges.
This is very likely the result of crushing inertia within DoD and the government in general, a problem many observers would affirm.
But it may also indicate less-than-heightened interest in Govini’s product. Given that the company is receiving approximately $80 million per year, that product should be expected to be of such value that it cannot be ignored.
Govini itself does not report or measure DoD success in making headway, either because there’s little to report or, as Dougherty opines, “that’s the Department’s story to tell – not Govini.”
Last fall’s revelation that China-sourced raw material for magnets used in the F-35 drove the Pentagon to temporarily suspend deliveries of the fighter while another material supplier was found is a sign of some progress Dougherty asserts.
But she notes that, “You can have all the statutory requirements not to buy from these companies. You can have executive orders saying we need to understand rare-earths supply chains and identify risk. But if you don’t mandate wholesale change to the people in acquisition, their behavior will only be marginally impacted.”
